title: "Testing the wind disruption hypothesis for beetle refugia"

abstract: >
  Mass attack by mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae) is coordinated by an airborne pheromone plume.
  Refugia are therefore hypothesised to form where stands are thin enough for wind to disrupt that plume. The
  mechanism has never been tested spatially. We test it across 168 km2 of inventoried forest and 1,740 m of relief
  in British Columbia, combining an aerial survey of beetle-caused mortality (1999-2015) with inventory host
  attributes and Global Wind Atlas speed.
  Attack is unimodal, peaking near 1,430 m. Below 1,900 m that peak is the distribution of lodgepole pine.
  Above 1,900 m it is not: attack halves while cover holds. Coding host as cover alone overstates that result.
  Attack rises monotonically with stand diameter, from 15 to 41 per cent across the range, with the steepest step
  at the 25 cm source-sink threshold the species' bionomics predicts, and the share of stands above that threshold
  falls four-fold at the top of the gradient. Conditioning on diameter and the remaining host terms removes about a
  quarter of the high-elevation suppression and leaves three quarters standing.
  We find no wind effect. Orthogonalised against a linear elevation term, wind is the strongest negative predictor
  in host-bearing stands and clears the interval test at every severity threshold above trace. But a unimodal
  response leaves elevation's curvature inside that term, and refitting elevation as a quadratic or spline collapses
  the coefficient everywhere. The signal is a specification artefact. Nor is the predictor the quantity the insect
  responds to: the atlas reports an annual mean at 10 m over open ground, while flight is arrested by instantaneous
  below-canopy speeds near 2 m s-1.
  Thermal alternatives survive. Deep-winter air temperature within 100 km never approaches the lethal range for
  overwintering late instars, but our coldest reading lies inside the range for early instars, 41 per cent of
  minima fall in December before hardening completes, and the record excludes the shoulder months entirely. Loss
  of univoltine development at elevation predicts the same pattern without invoking wind.
  Elevation explains 0.63 of the wind surface's variance landscape-wide but 0.80 within a 2 by 4 km clip, where the
  estimate reverses sign; grain scarcely matters. At the extent disturbance ecology usually adopts this study would
  have reported the opposite; with severity collapsed to presence, no result at all; and without a host layer,
  absence of pine misread as refugia.

```{r}
## past 1,000 m at the grid edge, where the 625 m window is truncated, and on a
## full-range ramp that artefact flattens the whole interior to one colour.
panel <- function(r, title, legend, pal = "viridis", dir = 1, q = c(.02, .98)) {
  lim <- unname(quantile(values(r, mat = FALSE), q, na.rm = TRUE))
  ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = pal, direction = dir, na.value = "grey88",
                         name = legend, limits = lim, oob = scales::squish) +
    clip_layer + study + labs(title = title, subtitle = sub_utm)
}
```

# Literature review {#sec-review}

The review below is written against this study's four objectives rather than as a survey of the
species, and its findings are numbered R1 to R5 and cited by number in every section that follows.
The protocol, the screening decisions and the per-study attribute extraction are recorded in
`02.inputs/literature/review-protocol.md`; every count reported here is computed at render time from
`02.inputs/literature/review-screening.csv` and none is typed into the prose.

```{r}
#| label: review-screen
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## The screening table is built by 02.inputs/literature/build-review-screening.py against the
## central store, and read here. Counts in the prose below are inline expressions over this
## object, so a change to the screening cannot leave the text behind.
rev  <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/literature/review-screening.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
inc  <- rev[rev$stage2_include == "yes", ]

N_CAND    <- nrow(rev)
N_INC     <- nrow(inc)
N_FULL    <- sum(inc$full_text_checked == "yes")
N_WIND    <- sum(inc$wind_predictor == "yes")
N_NOWIND  <- N_INC - N_WIND
WIND_WHO  <- inc$key[inc$wind_predictor == "yes"]
YR_RANGE  <- range(suppressWarnings(as.integer(inc$year)), na.rm = TRUE)

## Every included study was read in full text, because the review's central claim is an
## absence and an absence established from titles is not evidence.
stopifnot(N_FULL == N_INC)
```

## Search and screening

The corpus is the central store described in @sec-review-limits, holding 579 distinct papers at the
date of the search. Matching titles and filenames on *beetle*, *Dendroctonus*, *MPB*,
*Ips typographus*, *Scolytinae* and *refugi* returned `r N_CAND` candidates. A study was retained if
it models bark-beetle-caused tree mortality spatially against terrain, landscape or climate
predictors, which is the only design that can address objectives 1, 3 and 4. `r N_INC` studies
qualified, spanning `r YR_RANGE[1]` to `r YR_RANGE[2]`, and all `r N_FULL` were read in full text.

Excluded studies are not discarded. Papers on mechanism and physiology carry the life history the
Introduction rests on, and papers on detection carry the error properties of the response variable;
both are cited there. They are absent from the counts because they cannot answer the objectives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-review
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The studies retained by the review, with the attributes the objectives turn on, extracted from full text. The wind column records whether a wind term entered the model, not whether the word appears: every occurrence of `wind` in all eleven texts was read in context, and the per-study result is recorded in the review protocol."

inc |>
  transform(Study = ifelse(nzchar(key), key, "Zabihi 2021 (unverified)")) |>
  (\(d) d[order(suppressWarnings(as.integer(d$year))), ])() |>
  transform(Year = year,
            `Wind in model` = ifelse(wind_predictor == "yes", "yes", "no"),
            `Occurrences of \"wind\"` = wind_mentions,
            `Terrain terms` = terrain_terms,
            Pages = n_pages) |>
  subset(select = c("Study", "Year", "Terrain terms", "Wind in model",
                    "Occurrences of \"wind\"", "Pages")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "llccrr")
```

## Findings

**R1. The wind-disruption mechanism has been proposed but never fitted.** Of the `r N_INC` studies
that model bark beetle attack against terrain, `r N_WIND` enters a wind term, and that one is the
companion study on this same landscape whose response is conifer regeneration rather than beetle
attack [@murphy2026]. In the remaining `r N_NOWIND`, wind is either absent from the text entirely or
occurs only in a reference-list entry or a discussion sentence. @cartwright2018 is the clearest case:
the predictor set is slope, topographic position, heat load, compound topographic index and soil bulk
density, and wind appears three times, all in the discussion, invoked to explain an observed
thinner-stand association. @krawchuk2020 states the hypothesis and fits no model. The mechanism has
therefore been carried in this literature for at least `r YR_RANGE[2] - 2018` years as an
explanation, without once being entered as a predictor. Objective 3 addresses this directly.

**R2. The host-density half of the hypothesis already has support, and it is confounded.** The one
included study designed to identify insect refugia and model their controls found them associated
with thinner stands, shaded slopes and convergent topographic positions [@cartwright2018]. Thin
stands are exactly where a wind effect would be expected, and also where host is scarce, so the
association is consistent with the hypothesis and with its principal alternative. Separating them
requires an independent host layer, which is objective 1.

**R3. Host is never coded as the attribute the life history says matters.** None of the `r N_INC`
included studies mentions the 25 cm source-sink threshold or quadratic mean diameter, though the
threshold has been in the standard bionomics review since 2003 [@carroll2004bionomics]. Host enters
as cover, as basal area, or as a susceptibility class. Since brood production is governed by stem
size rather than by how much host is present, a host layer coded as cover cannot distinguish a stand
that produces beetles from one that consumes them. Objective 2 tests what changes when it is coded
as diameter instead.

**R4. Scale is recognised in this literature but conclusions are not tested against it.** Scale
vocabulary appears in six of the `r N_INC` included studies, so the issue is not unacknowledged, and
the included extents run from a single landscape to the whole of British Columbia. What the review
did not find is a study that refits one model across extent, grain and response coding on one dataset
and reports whether its own conclusion survives. Objective 4 does that, and @sec-extent, @sec-grain
and @sec-ordinal report the result.

**R5. No available wind product reports the quantity the hypothesis is about.** The hypothesis
concerns an instantaneous speed, below the canopy, during the July and August flight period, at the
height a beetle flies. Gridded products report a long-run mean at 10 m over open ground, and they are
produced by downscaling a coarse field over a digital elevation model [@badger2014; @davis2023],
which makes them partly a transform of the terrain they are offered alongside. The ceiling the
hypothesis leans on, about 2 m s⁻¹, is itself an inference across species
[@carroll2004bionomics; @jones2019]. Any test of objective 3 is therefore a test of a proxy, and the
review's conclusion is that the proxy's dependence on elevation has to be measured before its
coefficient can be read at all. R6 takes the same question along the time axis and reaches a
harder answer: not only does no product report the right quantity, no study says over what
interval the quantity should be reported.

```{r}
#| label: review-wind-temporal
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## The temporal resolution at which each included study treats wind, extracted from
## full text by 02.inputs/literature/extract-wind-temporal.py. Every wind sentence and
## its classification is written to wind-temporal-sentences.csv so any count below can
## be disputed against the sentence it came from. "window" and "windthrow" are excluded
## from the match, as they are in the screening table: a first run without that
## exclusion returned six wind mentions in @haukema2008movement that were all the
## phrase "temporal window".
wt <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/literature/wind-temporal-summary.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

WT_N       <- nrow(wt)
WT_SILENT  <- sum(wt$n_wind == 0)
WT_SCALED  <- sum(nzchar(wt$finest))
WT_UNSCALED<- WT_N - WT_SCALED
WT_MENTION <- WT_N - WT_SILENT          # studies that use the word at all
WT_M_UNSC  <- WT_MENTION - WT_SCALED    # of those, how many say nothing about time
WT_KRAW    <- wt$n_wind[grepl("krawchuk", wt$study)]   # the study that states the hypothesis
WT_WHO     <- wt$study[nzchar(wt$finest)]
WT_MAX     <- wt$study[which.max(wt$n_wind)]
WT_MAXN    <- max(wt$n_wind)
stopifnot(WT_N == N_INC)
## the single study carrying temporal vocabulary must be the companion paper; if a
## future corpus adds another, R6's wording has to change rather than silently mislead
stopifnot(WT_SCALED == 1, grepl("murphy", WT_MAX))
```

**R6. The literature specifies no temporal resolution for wind, so the choice cannot be
deferred to it.** The analysis in this study has to decide what wind means in a model: a
long-run climatology, a growing-season mean, a monthly mean, a flight-window statistic
or an hourly series are five different covariates and they do not agree with each other.
Reading every wind sentence in the full text of all `r WT_N` included studies settles
where the literature stands, and the answer is that it does not stand anywhere.
`r WT_SILENT` of the `r WT_N` do not contain the word at all once "window" and
"windthrow" are excluded. Of the `r WT_MENTION` that do use it, `r WT_M_UNSC` attach no
temporal vocabulary to it whatsoever: no averaging period, no season, no time of day.
Across the whole included set that is `r WT_UNSCALED` of `r WT_N` studies silent on the
question. The single exception is @murphy2026, with `r WT_MAXN` mentions carrying monthly and annual
vocabulary, and that is the companion study on this same landscape, which took mean
monthly speeds at 10 m for 2015 to 2020 from the Global Wind Atlas [@murphy2026] and so
described a period five to fifteen years after the outbreak it was modelling.
@krawchuk2020, who state the hypothesis, mention wind `r WT_KRAW` times and never once say over
what interval it should be measured.

The consequence for this study is a positive one and it is the reason R6 exists. Because
no prior specification can be cited, the temporal resolution has to be argued from the
mechanism rather than adopted from precedent, and the mechanism is explicit about it:
dispersal and pheromone-mediated mass attack happen during a narrow midsummer flight
period, and within it they depend on whether the air is still enough to hold a plume.
That argues for the finest resolution the observations support, reduced only at the last
step into the flight window itself. @sec-krawchuk reports what is used and what it costs.

## Limits of this review {#sec-review-limits}

The corpus is one curated library rather than a systematic search of an abstracting database, so
this is a review of what was read, made checkable, rather than a claim about the complete
literature. A study that entered a wind predictor and is absent from the store would not have been
found, and R1 carries that scope wherever it is used. The screening table records the decision and
the extracted attribute for every candidate so that a reader can dispute either.

# Introduction

Disturbance refugia, defined by @krawchuk2020 as locations "disturbed less severely or less frequently than other areas within the surrounding landscape", have become an organising concept in forest conservation under a changing climate. The framework identifies where biological legacies persist through a disturbance and why those legacies matter to the recovery of the surrounding stand. Its empirical base is predominantly a wildfire literature [@krawchuk2020; @littlefield2019]. For insect outbreaks the base is thinner: @krawchuk2020 observe that few studies have explicitly identified refugia from insect outbreaks, even though the stand and landscape controls on outbreak severity are themselves well documented for the better-studied pests.

For mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus ponderosae* Hopkins), @krawchuk2020 advance three hypotheses. Refugia might occur, first, in areas with cooler temperatures, for example from topographic shading, that protect trees from water stress; second, in areas of lower host density, "allowing for greater wind disruption of beetle pheromone communication and more vigorous tree growth and chemical defenses"; and third, in areas with fewer large-diameter host trees, or among trees investing more heavily in resistance traits such as resin ducts. These are not mutually exclusive. All three predict reduced attack on high, cool, sparsely stocked ground, and they are separable only by the mechanism each invokes. The present study tests the second hypothesis and treats the first and third as the competing explanations against which it must be judged.

@cartwright2018 provides the closest existing test. Working at 30 m resolution in lodgepole and whitebark pine in southern Oregon, that study identified refugia from Landsat moisture anomalies during a concurrent 2009 drought and beetle outbreak, and modelled their landscape controls. Refugia were associated with shaded slopes, convergent topographic positions, low soil bulk density and thinner stands. The thinner-stand association is consistent with the host-density component of the second hypothesis, but no wind surface was available and the disruption mechanism itself was not evaluated. The review in @sec-review makes that observation countable rather than rhetorical: of the studies that model bark beetle attack against terrain, one enters a wind term and it is the companion study on the present landscape (R1).

## Beetle life history

Interpreting any spatial pattern of attack requires the population biology that generates it. Mountain pine beetle populations occupy one of four phases defined by population size relative to available host: endemic, incipient epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic [@safranyik2006chap1]. Endemic populations persist in weakened, generally small-diameter trees. Incipient-epidemic populations develop when larger-diameter hosts become colonisable, through a local decline in host resistance, immigration, or favourable breeding conditions. Epidemics operate at landscape scale and arise mainly from extensive, contiguous areas of susceptible host under favourable weather [@safranyik2006chap1]. The transition between phases is a density-dependent threshold rather than a gradient: @howe2022 show that stand-level spatial aggregation, behavioural shifts and the quality of attainable hosts converge to define a critical threshold beyond which population growth becomes self-driving. Outbreak history in British Columbia has been governed jointly by the availability of susceptible age classes and by climate [@taylor2003; @sambaraju2021].

Colonisation proceeds by mass attack, which is a density phenomenon rather than a behaviour. A lodgepole pine resists a single beetle through constitutive resin flow and an induced response that saturates the phloem with terpenes, and the constitutive terpene profile itself varies geographically in ways that correlate with historical attack [@clark2010]. Overwhelming that defence requires the near-simultaneous arrival of many individuals, and the arrival is coordinated chemically. Pioneer females oxidise the host monoterpene α-pinene to *trans*-verbenol, which is preferentially attractive to males; arriving males release *exo*-brevicomin, which at low concentrations attracts mainly females; and the host kairomones α-pinene and myrcene synergise both, so that colonisation of a tree is normally completed within one to two days [@safranyik2006chap1]. At approximately 60 attacks per square metre of bark the signal reverses. High concentrations of *exo*-brevicomin and frontalin, together with the anti-aggregation pheromone verbenone, terminate colonisation and redirect arrivals to neighbouring trees [@safranyik2006chap1]. Because this signal is airborne, it is in principle susceptible to disruption by wind, and that susceptibility is the premise of the hypothesis under test.

Host quality sets a second constraint, and it is a constraint on stem size rather than on host abundance. Bark roughness, bark thickness, bark surface area, phloem thickness and sapwood moisture retention all increase with tree diameter, and together they determine how many beetles a colonised tree can produce. @carroll2004bionomics summarise the consequence as a threshold: on average, lodgepole pine trees of 25 cm diameter or less are beetle sinks, in that more beetles attack than emerge, whereas trees above 25 cm are beetle sources. The threshold is stated for individual trees. We apply it to a stand-level attribute, quadratic mean diameter, and therefore treat it as an approximate ordering of stand suitability rather than as a per-stand criterion transferred intact from the source.

Temperature imposes the third and fourth constraints, and they act on different parts of the life cycle. Dispersal is bounded by a flight envelope. @carroll2004bionomics summarise it as lower and upper limits of 19 and 41 °C after @mccambridge1971, with most beetles flying between 22 and 32 °C after Safranyik, negative phototaxis above 35 °C and severely restricted flight above 38 °C. The primary measurement behind the outer bounds was made on beetles reared from field-infested ponderosa pine and tested at 50 per cent relative humidity without direct insolation: @mccambridge1971 places the threshold at approximately 67 to 68 °F, or 19 to 20 °C, and extrapolates an upper limit near 107 °F, or 42 °C. That study also records field flight below its own laboratory threshold where sunlight warms emerged beetles or the bark around them, so the laboratory envelope is a conservative bound on ambient air temperature rather than a hard limit.

Development is bounded separately. Stage-specific development thresholds maintain synchrony within and among seasons, and sub-population-specific development rates maintain univoltinism across much of the species range [@safranyik2006chap1]. Where heat accumulation is insufficient, as at high elevation and near the northern range margin, populations become semivoltine. Stretching the life cycle across two years imposes severe mortality, because the insect must overwinter twice, often in cold-susceptible stages, and remains exposed to natural enemies for longer [@safranyik2006chap1]. In semivoltine populations, climate becomes the dominant control on distribution and abundance.

Overwinter survival is bounded by cold tolerance, which is acquired rather than fixed. Glycerol accumulates in the hemolymph as temperatures decline through autumn, so cold-hardiness is greatest from December to February and is incomplete on either side of that window [@safranyik2006chap1]. Tolerance also varies by stage. Lethal temperature ranges have been estimated at -18 °C for eggs, -18 to -34 °C for pupae, -23 to -34 °C for adults, and, for larvae, -23 to -29 °C for first instars, -23 to -34 °C for second instars and -29 to -40 °C for third and fourth instars [@safranyik2006chap1]. Late larval instars are the normal overwintering stage and withstand temperatures near -40 °C for extended midwinter periods, which is the origin of the conventionally quoted lethal figure. The same source is explicit that a midwinter minimum of -30 °C would be expected to cause little mortality, and that significant mortality instead follows cold arriving early, before sufficient glycerol has accumulated, or late, after it has begun to be metabolised. Any assessment of thermal limitation on a landscape therefore depends on the date of the minimum as much as on its depth, a point we return to in @sec-cold.

## Wind and flight

The wind-disruption hypothesis requires wind to interfere with the pheromone plume. A second and simpler route from wind to reduced attack acts on the insect directly, by suppressing flight, and the two cannot be separated by the design used here. The standard figure is a wind ceiling of about 2 m s⁻¹. @carroll2004bionomics state it directly: bark beetles in general do not fly in winds exceeding their maximum flight speed, and for a large-bodied species such as mountain pine beetle the maximum wind speed for flight, and so the probable maximum flight velocity, is approximately 2 m s⁻¹. The provenance of that number is worth stating, because it is an inference across species rather than a measurement on this one: the primary citation is a study of *Dendroctonus pseudotsugae* Hopkins. The comparative evidence assembled by @jones2019 is consistent but no firmer. *Dendroctonus frontalis* Zimmermann cannot fly above 2 m s⁻¹, *Ips pini* Say and *Scolytus multistriatus* Marsham arrest flight at 4.8 and 5 km h⁻¹, and in the one laboratory wind tunnel trial on *D. ponderosae* the beetles flew for longer at 0, 0.5 and 1 m s⁻¹ than at 2 m s⁻¹, which is a reduction in flight duration rather than arrest. Flight-mill velocities for *D. ponderosae* are reported in the same review as 1.55 to 1.93 km h⁻¹, or roughly 0.43 to 0.54 m s⁻¹, with mean flight distances of 2.12 to 5.95 km, so the ceiling is several times the sustained cruising speed. Dispersal is also density-dependent, switching between short-range movement below the canopy and long-range transport above it as population density rises [@powell2014; @johnson2026density; @johnson2026stratified]. At low wind speeds the dispersal direction of *D. ponderosae* is not influenced by wind direction [@jones2019].

## Measurement problems

Testing the hypothesis requires a spatial wind surface, and the available surfaces carry three properties that constrain what can be inferred from them.

The first is construction. Gridded wind products, including the Global Wind Atlas, are produced by driving a mesoscale model from reanalysis, generalising the output to remove local terrain and roughness effects, and then downscaling it over a digital elevation model and a land-cover roughness map [@badger2014; @davis2023]. Elevation is an input to the product rather than a covariate measured independently of it. A wind surface entered into a model alongside elevation is therefore not an independent measurement, and the degree of dependence is a function of study extent, because a coarse driving field is close to flat over a few kilometres and almost all within-product variation at small extents derives from terrain. The extents at which disturbance ecology commonly works, a burn perimeter or a cluster of field plots, are the extents at which this dependence is most severe and least visible.

The second is correspondence to the biological quantity. The hypothesis concerns an instantaneous speed, below the canopy, during the July and August flight period, at the height at which beetles fly. The atlas reports an annual mean at 10 m above open ground. The two quantities differ in height, season, averaging period and canopy position, and no downscaled product currently available at landscape scale reports the former.

The third is a confound specific to refugia work. A cell recorded as unattacked may simply contain no host. In the terms of @krawchuk2020 this is the distinction between what a location is a refugium from and what it is a refugium for, and it cannot be resolved without an independent map of host abundance. The precedent is direct: @hadley1994 predicted heavier beetle-caused mortality on hot, dry, south-facing slopes and observed the reverse, because host distribution rather than moisture stress governed where attack succeeded. We extend the argument by noting that a map of host cover is also insufficient, because the attribute governing whether a stand produces beetles is stem diameter rather than cover.

## Objectives

Each question below follows from a numbered finding of the review in @sec-review, and the finding it answers is named with it. We address four questions on a single landscape spanning `r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief.

1.  **From R2.** Does terrain condition beetle-caused mortality once host abundance is accounted for, and at what point on the elevation gradient does host distribution cease to explain the observed pattern? The review found the host-density half of the hypothesis supported but confounded with the wind half, and separable only with an independent host layer.
2.  **From R3.** Does that result survive coding host as stem diameter rather than as cover, given the 25 cm source-sink threshold reported for individual trees by @carroll2004bionomics? No study retained by the review codes host as the attribute the life history says governs brood production.
3.  **From R1 and R5.** Does the component of the wind surface that is independent of elevation predict reduced attack where host is present, as hypothesised by @krawchuk2020? The review found the mechanism proposed repeatedly and fitted once, in a companion study with a different response, and found that no available product reports the wind quantity the hypothesis concerns.
4.  **From R4.** To what extent does the answer to question 3 depend on analytical decisions that are not fixed by the data: the extent of the study area, the grain of the analysis cells, and whether damage is coded as a binary outcome or as the ordinal severity class the survey records? Scale is acknowledged in this literature without any retained study refitting one model across all three axes and reporting whether its conclusion survives.

The fourth question is answered by refitting the same response, predictors and model across each axis in turn: across the full landscape and within a 2 by 4 km clip drawn from it, at 25 m, 50 m and 100 m grain, and at each severity threshold. Two of the three axes alter the conclusion.

# Materials

## Study area

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the South Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. The terrain grid spans 16 by 17.5 km and `r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief, from valley bottom to alpine. The modelled area is a subset, because cells carrying no inventory basal area cannot enter a model conditioning on stand structure; @tbl-relief reports its extent and relief. The two extents are distinct and are not interchangeable. The range crosses the full biogeoclimatic sequence of the southern interior wet belt, from the dry warm Interior Cedar-Hemlock subzones through the moist warm subzones to the Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir zone and its parkland variant [@ketcheson1991; @braumandl2005]. Lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta* var. *latifolia*), the beetle's principal host here, occupies the middle of that sequence and is scarce at both ends.

The site description and terrain surfaces are inherited from a companion analysis of conifer regeneration on the same ground [@murphy2026], which used them to predict seedling intensity after a 2015 wildfire. Disturbance was a predictor there; here it is the response. @fig-site locates the landscape and shows the three spatial inputs.

## Beetle-caused mortality

```{r}
#| label: read-response
#| echo: true

aos_box <- ext(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005"))
aos <- vect(here("02.inputs/aos/pest_infestation_poly.gdb"),
            layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = aos_box)
mpb <- project(aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM", ], crs(G))   # IBM = mountain pine beetle
m   <- mpb[mpb$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]

## BC severity classes are ordinal: trace, light, moderate, severe, very severe
sev_rank <- c(T = 1, L = 2, M = 3, S = 4, V = 5)
m$sev <- unname(sev_rank[m$PEST_SEVERITY_CODE]); m$sev[is.na(m$sev)] <- 0

severity  <- rasterize(m, G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)

c(polygons = nrow(m), years = length(unique(m$CAPTURE_YEAR)),
  hectares = round(sum(m$AREA_HA)))
```

The response is the British Columbia Aerial Overview Survey, the operational provincial record of forest health, in which observers sketch-map damage annually from aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species. We take polygons coded `IBM`, mountain pine beetle, for the outbreak window 1999 to 2015, and rasterise the maximum severity class reached by each cell.

The survey was preferred to a spectral classification for a specific reason. Red attack has been mapped from Landsat with improving accuracy [@white2005; @meddens2013; @ye2021], but every such product is a model whose errors are spatially structured and not independent of terrain, because illumination, shadow and view angle vary with slope and aspect. For a question about terrain, a response from a terrain-sensitive classifier risks recovering the classifier's own terrain sensitivity. Sketch-mapping has cruder errors, but they are observer errors, not errors generated by the predictors under test.

The severity scale is anchored to ground measurement. Twenty-eight field plots established in beetle-affected stands in 2020 recorded the basal area of pine killed, spanning 0.6 to 47.4 m2/ha, or 1.3 to 94.7 per cent of plot basal area, and calibrated the spectral mapping used in the companion study [@murphy2026]. Plot coordinates were not recoverable, so the plots calibrate the severity scale but cannot verify the spatial placement of individual polygons. No validation of polygon placement is therefore claimed.

@fig-site shows the landscape and the response together. Panel (b) is the elevation surface that defines the grid and panel (d) the survey record this paper models: attack concentrated in a mid-elevation band, sparse in the valley and again along the alpine crest. Panel (c) is the wind surface whose relationship to that terrain the second half of the paper is about.

```{r}

#| fig-height: 6.8

(c) Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m; the shaded southern band lies outside the wind product's extent. (d) Beetle-caused mortality from the Aerial Overview Survey, 1999 to 2015, as the maximum severity class in any year. The outlined rectangle in (b) to (d) is the 2 by 4 km clip of @sec-extent. Each panel's graticule, axis ticks and stated coordinate reference system are the same; the system is named beneath the panel title and ticks are in kilometres."

prov <- st_transform(ne_states(country = c("Canada","United States of America"),

## BC is framed to the analysis grid's aspect ratio so the two rows of the figure are

b0 <- st_bbox(prov[prov$name == "British Columbia", ]); tgt <- unname(gw/gh)
w0 <- unname(b0["xmax"]-b0["xmin"]); h0 <- unname(b0["ymax"]-b0["ymin"])

if (w0/h0 > tgt) h0 <- w0/tgt else w0 <- h0*tgt

sev_f <- as.factor(severity)
```

## Red-stage classification

The aerial overview survey resolves damage at the scale an observer can sketch
from an aircraft, and the refugia question is about wind and terrain acting at
tens of metres. So we also classified red-stage attack annually from Landsat
across the whole grid, to see whether a finer response layer would support the
test that the polygons cannot. The pipeline below is that classification. Its
result is reported here rather than in Results because it decides which response
layer the paper uses, and the answer is that it does not replace the survey.

Every stage runs in Google Earth Engine through `rgee`. The code is gated on the
exported rasters: where they are absent it builds and downloads them, which takes
roughly half an hour, and where they are present the render reads them and needs
no network. Function definitions sit outside the gate so they are readable
whether or not they run.

```{r}
#| label: ee-pipeline-setup
#| echo: true

RED_DIR   <- here("02.inputs/beetle-classification/red-stage")
BASE_YEAR <- 2003          # differencing baseline, see below
CLASS_YRS <- 2005:2014
dec_files <- file.path(RED_DIR, sprintf("dec_%d.tif", CLASS_YRS))

## Sensor supplying each year, taken from Landsat scene metadata rather than
## from the parent study's Table 2, which lists Landsat 5 for a 2013 acquisition.
## Landsat 5 stopped acquiring in November 2011 and Landsat 8 did not begin until
## 2013, so 2012 is the one year only Landsat 7 covers. The parent study omitted
## 2012 for that reason and not for cloud: six Landsat 7 scenes met its own
## selection rule of under 20 per cent cloud between 1 June and 30 August, the
## cleanest at 1 per cent. Landsat 7 has flown scan-line-corrector-off since May
## 2003, so that year alone carries striping. Inventory in
## 02.inputs/beetle-classification/landsat-scene-inventory.csv.
SENSOR <- c(`2003`="LT05",`2005`="LT05",`2006`="LT05",`2007`="LT05",`2008`="LT05",
            `2009`="LT05",`2010`="LT05",`2011`="LT05",`2012`="LE07",
            `2013`="LC08",`2014`="LC08")
COLL   <- c(LT05="LANDSAT/LT05/C02/T1_L2", LE07="LANDSAT/LE07/C02/T1_L2",
            LC08="LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
SB     <- c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")
BANDS  <- c(SB, "NDMI", "dNDMI")
```

```{r}
#| label: ee-pipeline-functions
#| echo: true

## Stage 1, imagery. Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance, scaled by the
## published factors, with cloud, cloud shadow, cirrus and snow masked from
## QA_PIXEL bits 1 to 5. Thematic Mapper and Enhanced Thematic Mapper carry the
## reflective bands as SR_B1-5 and SR_B7; the Operational Land Imager shifts them
## to SR_B2-7 because it adds a coastal aerosol band. Both are renamed to common
## names so nothing downstream has to know which sensor it is reading.
ee_prep <- function(sensor) {
  bn <- if (sensor == "LC08") paste0("SR_B", 2:7) else paste0("SR_B", c(1:5, 7))
  rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(function(im) {
    qa   <- im$select("QA_PIXEL")
    keep <- qa$bitwiseAnd(2L)$eq(0)$And(qa$bitwiseAnd(4L)$eq(0))$
      And(qa$bitwiseAnd(8L)$eq(0))$And(qa$bitwiseAnd(16L)$eq(0))$
      And(qa$bitwiseAnd(32L)$eq(0))
    im$select(bn, SB)$multiply(0.0000275)$add(-0.2)$updateMask(keep)$
      copyProperties(im, list("SUN_ELEVATION","SUN_AZIMUTH","system:time_start"))
  })
}

ee_year <- function(y, AOI) {
  s <- SENSOR[[as.character(y)]]
  ee$ImageCollection(COLL[[s]])$filterBounds(AOI)$
    filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-08-31", y))$
    filter(ee$Filter$lt("CLOUD_COVER", 60))$map(ee_prep(s))
}

## Stage 2, terrain correction. Mandatory here and not at the 7.78 km2 extent the
## parent study worked at. Across 1,776 m of relief, illumination varies enough
## with slope and aspect to put a terrain signal into reflectance, and this study
## tests terrain effects, so an uncorrected artefact would be indistinguishable
## from the result. SCS+C after Soenen et al. 2005: the C term is the ratio of
## intercept to slope in a regression of reflectance on the illumination term,
## fitted per band per scene. Where a scene is wholly masked over the grid the
## regression returns null; C is then set very large, which drives the correction
## factor to one, so a scene with nothing to fit is passed through unchanged
## rather than destroyed.
ee_illum <- function(im, slope, asp) {
  sz <- ee$Image$constant(90)$subtract(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_ELEVATION")))$multiply(pi/180)
  sa <- ee$Image$constant(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_AZIMUTH")))$multiply(pi/180)
  slope$cos()$multiply(sz$cos())$
    add(slope$sin()$multiply(sz$sin())$multiply(sa$subtract(asp)$cos()))$rename("cos_i")
}

ee_scs_c <- function(im, slope, asp, AOI) {
  ci <- ee_illum(im, slope, asp)
  sz <- ee$Image$constant(90)$subtract(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_ELEVATION")))$multiply(pi/180)
  n0 <- slope$cos()$multiply(sz$cos())
  one <- function(b) {
    f  <- ci$addBands(im$select(b))$reduceRegion(ee$Reducer$linearFit(), AOI, 90,
                                                 maxPixels = 1e9, bestEffort = TRUE)
    sc <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(f$get("scale"),  f$get("scale"),  0))
    of <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(f$get("offset"), f$get("offset"), 0))
    C  <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(sc$abs()$gt(1e-8), of$divide(sc), 1e6))$max(0)$min(1e6)
    im$select(b)$multiply(n0$add(C))$divide(ci$add(C))$rename(b)
  }
  bs <- one(SB[1]); for (b in SB[-1]) bs <- bs$addBands(one(b))
  bs$copyProperties(im, list("SUN_ELEVATION","SUN_AZIMUTH","system:time_start"))
}

## Stage 3, index and differencing. NDMI is (NIR - SWIR1) / (NIR + SWIR1) and each
## annual composite is differenced against the pre-outbreak baseline. The baseline
## is 2003, not the 2005 the parent study's text names twice. Its own Table 2
## labels 2003 pre-outbreak and 2005 early-outbreak, and its 2005 raster carries
## 534 cells coded red attack, 9.73 per cent of the cells it maps. A scene
## differenced against itself is zero everywhere, so 2005 cannot be its own
## baseline. See 02.inputs/beetle-classification/02-parent-raster-audit.R.
ee_stack <- function(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI) {
  m  <- ee_year(y, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
          function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()
  nd <- m$normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")
  m$addBands(nd)$addBands(nd$subtract(BASE)$rename("dNDMI"))
}
```

The classifier is trained on the aerial overview survey itself. The parent
study's 310-row spectral sample cannot be reused: every band column in the source
workbook is prefixed 2020, the plots were established in July and August 2020,
and the values sit inside the Collection 2 Level-1 range of the 2020 Landsat 8
scene, reading as negative reflectance in four bands if taken as Level-2. A model
built from one uncorrected 2020 scene was applied to map attack from 2005 to
2014, eight of those years from a different satellite. The plot coordinates are
also unrecoverable, so the spectra cannot be re-extracted on a matching footing.
Training on the survey instead keeps labels and imagery in the same year and the
same radiometry.

```{r}
#| label: ee-classify
#| echo: true

SAMP_FILE <- file.path(RED_DIR, "training-sample.csv")

## Stage 4, labels. Positives are cells the survey mapped at moderate severity or
## worse in that year, negatives cells it mapped as undamaged, 250 of each per
## year with a quarter held out. 2014 takes the pooled model because the survey
## records no cell above trace over this grid that year.
##
## The sample is written to disk and the classifier is then trained from the
## table rather than from the sampling graph. That is not tidiness. An Earth
## Engine classifier carries its training computation into every image it is
## later applied to, so classifying an annual composite from a classifier trained
## directly on nine years of sampled composites re-runs all of it and the
## download fails with a 400. Trained from stored numbers, the same download
## succeeds.
if (!file.exists(SAMP_FILE)) {
  library(rgee); ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  dir.create(RED_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  AOI   <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(-116.7861, 49.0884, -116.5649, 49.2460))
  DEM   <- ee$Image("USGS/SRTMGL1_003")
  slope <- ee$Terrain$slope(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  asp   <- ee$Terrain$aspect(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  BASE  <- ee_year(BASE_YEAR, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
             function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()$
             normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")

  set.seed(42); parts <- list()
  for (y in 2005:2013) {
    ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev",
                    fun = "max", background = 0)
    if (global(ry >= 3, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]] < 30) next
    pick <- function(mk, lab) {
      p <- spatSample(mk, 250, "random", na.rm = TRUE, xy = TRUE, values = FALSE)
      data.frame(x = p[,1], y = p[,2], lab = lab,
                 elev = extract(G, p[,1:2])[,1], yr = y)
    }
    d <- rbind(pick(ifel(ry >= 3, 1, NA), 1L), pick(ifel(ry == 0, 1, NA), 0L))
    d <- d[!is.na(d$elev), ]
    d$split <- as.integer(runif(nrow(d)) < 0.25)
    pts <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(d, coords = c("x","y"), crs = crs(G)), 4326)
    parts[[length(parts) + 1]] <- ee_stack(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI)$sampleRegions(
      collection = sf_as_ee(pts), properties = list("lab","elev","yr","split"),
      scale = 30, tileScale = 4, geometries = TRUE)
  }
  got <- ee_as_sf(ee$FeatureCollection(parts)$flatten(), quiet = TRUE)
  xy  <- sf::st_coordinates(got)
  write.csv(cbind(sf::st_drop_geometry(got), lon = xy[,1], lat = xy[,2]),
            SAMP_FILE, row.names = FALSE)
}
samp <- read.csv(SAMP_FILE)
stopifnot(all(c(BANDS, "lab", "elev", "yr", "split", "lon", "lat") %in% names(samp)))

## Stage 4b, the classifier. Fitted here rather than by ee$Classifier$libsvm,
## for a mechanical reason. An Earth Engine classifier carries its training
## features into every request that uses it, so each annual download embedded the
## whole labelled table and returned HTTP 400; the same eight-band composite
## downloads without complaint on its own. A linear kernel is a plane, so the
## fitted model transfers exactly as a band expression and Earth Engine is left
## doing arithmetic. The check below is that transfer, and it holds to machine
## precision. Predictors are standardised on the training rows only.
SVM_TR <- samp[samp$split == 0, ]; SVM_TE <- samp[samp$split == 1, ]
SVM_MU <- sapply(SVM_TR[BANDS], mean); SVM_SD <- sapply(SVM_TR[BANDS], sd)
zscore <- function(d) as.matrix(sweep(sweep(d[BANDS], 2, SVM_MU, "-"), 2, SVM_SD, "/"))
set.seed(1)
SVM_FIT <- kernlab::ksvm(zscore(SVM_TR), factor(SVM_TR$lab), type = "C-svc",
                         kernel = "vanilladot", C = 1, scaled = FALSE)
SVM_W <- colSums(kernlab::coef(SVM_FIT)[[1]] * kernlab::xmatrix(SVM_FIT)[[1]])
SVM_B <- -SVM_FIT@b
stopifnot(identical(
  as.integer(as.vector(zscore(SVM_TE) %*% SVM_W + SVM_B) > 0),
  as.integer(as.character(predict(SVM_FIT, zscore(SVM_TE))))))

## Collapsed into raw reflectance units, which is the form Earth Engine applies.
SVM_A <- SVM_W / SVM_SD
SVM_C <- SVM_B - sum(SVM_W * SVM_MU / SVM_SD)
stopifnot(max(abs((as.matrix(SVM_TE[BANDS]) %*% SVM_A + SVM_C) -
                  (zscore(SVM_TE) %*% SVM_W + SVM_B))) < 1e-8)

## Stage 5, validation. Computed here from the held-out quarter, so the agreement
## table below and the exported rasters come from one fitted object.
SVM_TE$pred <- as.integer(as.vector(as.matrix(SVM_TE[BANDS]) %*% SVM_A + SVM_C) > 0)

if (!all(file.exists(dec_files))) {
  library(rgee); ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  AOI   <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(-116.7861, 49.0884, -116.5649, 49.2460))
  DEM   <- ee$Image("USGS/SRTMGL1_003")
  slope <- ee$Terrain$slope(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  asp   <- ee$Terrain$aspect(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  BASE  <- ee_year(BASE_YEAR, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
             function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()$
             normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")

  ## Stage 6, export. The decision plane is applied band by band, thresholded at
  ## zero, classified at the 30 m native grid, then resampled onto the analysis
  ## grid by nearest neighbour, which is the correct rule for a class raster and
  ## makes the alignment exact rather than nearly so.
  gbox <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(xmin(G), ymin(G), xmax(G), ymax(G)),
                                proj = "EPSG:32611", geodesic = FALSE)
  for (y in CLASS_YRS) {
    st <- ee_stack(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI)
    d  <- ee$Image$constant(SVM_C)
    for (bn in BANDS) d <- d$add(st$select(bn)$multiply(unname(SVM_A[bn])))
    ## The continuous decision value is exported, not a thresholded map, so the
    ## threshold stays a visible choice made below rather than one baked into a
    ## download. Scaled by 1,000 and offset by 10,000 because a GeoTIFF written
    ## from an integer image takes zero as its nodata value: exporting a signed
    ## surface directly would silently delete every cell sitting on the decision
    ## boundary, and exporting a 0/1 map deleted every unattacked cell outright
    ## on the first attempt, returning 100 per cent attacked in all ten years.
    u <- d$multiply(1000)$add(10000)$round()$toInt16()$rename("dec")$
      getDownloadURL(list(name = sprintf("dec_%d", y), crs = "EPSG:32611",
                          scale = 30, region = gbox, format = "GEO_TIFF"))
    tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".tif"); download.file(u, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
    ## Kept in the scaled integer form Earth Engine sent, deflated, because the
    ## same surface as 32-bit float is 2.2 MB a year and this is 0.2 MB. The
    ## offset is removed at read time below, not here.
    writeRaster(resample(rast(tmp), G, method = "bilinear"),
                file.path(RED_DIR, sprintf("dec_%d.tif", y)),
                overwrite = TRUE, datatype = "INT2S",
                gdal = c("COMPRESS=DEFLATE", "PREDICTOR=2"))
  }
}

dec <- (rast(dec_files) - 10000) / 1000     # undo the export scaling and offset
names(dec) <- CLASS_YRS

## The model's own threshold is zero, which is what a balanced training sample
## implies. It is the wrong prior for this landscape. Training drew 250 attacked
## and 250 unattacked cells per year, so the implied prevalence is one half,
## while the survey maps attack on a few per cent of the grid. Thresholded at
## zero the classification calls a third to two thirds of the landscape attacked.
## Both maps are therefore carried: the model's own, and one whose threshold is
## calibrated per year so the classified area matches the area the survey mapped.
SURV_AREA <- sapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)
  global(ry >= 3, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
})
names(SURV_AREA) <- CLASS_YRS
RAW_AREA <- sapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y)
  global(dec[[as.character(y)]] > 0, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])
names(RAW_AREA) <- CLASS_YRS

red <- rast(lapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  d <- dec[[as.character(y)]]
  thr <- if (SURV_AREA[[as.character(y)]] > 0)
    global(d, function(v, ...) quantile(v, 1 - SURV_AREA[[as.character(y)]], na.rm = TRUE))[[1]]
    else Inf
  d > thr
}))
names(red) <- CLASS_YRS
## A classification that is entirely one class, or entirely masked, is a
## pipeline failure rather than a result, and must not reach the prose.
stopifnot(nlyr(red) == length(CLASS_YRS),
          all(dim(red)[1:2] == dim(G)[1:2]),
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(ext(red)), as.vector(ext(G)), tolerance = 1e-6)),
          all(RAW_AREA > 0.001), all(RAW_AREA < 0.999),
          all(global(!is.na(red), "mean")[[1]] > 0.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-redstage
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between the Landsat red-stage classification and the aerial overview survey, by 300 m elevation band. The held-out quarter of the labelled sample, pooled over 2005 to 2013. This is agreement with the survey, not accuracy against ground truth: the survey is also the training source, and no independent reference exists at this extent."

v <- SVM_TE
v$classification <- v$pred
v$band <- cut(v$elev, seq(500, 2400, by = 300), dig.lab = 5)

kap <- function(o, p) {
  cm <- table(factor(o, 0:1), factor(p, 0:1))
  oa <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
  pe <- sum(rowSums(cm) * colSums(cm)) / sum(cm)^2
  c(OA = oa, kappa = (oa - pe) / (1 - pe))
}
POOLED <- kap(v$lab, v$classification)

RED_TBL <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(v$band), function(b) {
  s <- v[!is.na(v$band) & v$band == b, ]
  if (nrow(s) < 10)
    return(data.frame(Band = b, n = nrow(s), Attacked = sum(s$lab == 1),
                      Agreement = NA_real_, Kappa = NA_real_,
                      Note = "too few reference points, uncertain"))
  k <- kap(s$lab, s$classification)
  data.frame(Band = b, n = nrow(s), Attacked = sum(s$lab == 1),
             Agreement = round(k["OA"], 3), Kappa = round(k["kappa"], 3), Note = "")
}))
kable(RED_TBL, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Elevation band (m)", "n", "Attacked", "Agreement", "Kappa", ""))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-redstage-area
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Where the Landsat classification and the aerial overview survey disagree, by year. Survey area is the share of the grid the survey mapped at moderate severity or worse. Model area is what the classifier calls attacked at its own threshold of zero. Hit rate is the share of calibrated classified cells that fall inside a survey polygon, and lift is that rate divided by the survey's own prevalence, so 1.00 is chance."

RED_CMP <- do.call(rbind, lapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  yc <- as.character(y)
  ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)
  S  <- ry >= 3
  p  <- SURV_AREA[[yc]]
  if (p == 0) return(data.frame(Year = y, Survey = 0, Model = round(100*RAW_AREA[[yc]], 1),
                                Hit = NA_real_, Lift = NA_real_))
  hits <- global(S & red[[yc]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
  nC   <- global(red[[yc]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
  data.frame(Year = y, Survey = round(100*p, 3), Model = round(100*RAW_AREA[[yc]], 1),
             Hit = round(100*hits/nC, 2), Lift = round((hits/nC)/p, 2))
}))
kable(RED_CMP, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Year", "Survey area (%)", "Model area (%)",
                    "Hit rate (%)", "Lift"))
```

The classification does not replace the survey, and the reason is not a marginal
shortfall in accuracy. Pooled over the held-out quarter it agrees with the survey
on `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * POOLED["OA"])` per cent of cells, kappa
`r sprintf("%.2f", POOLED["kappa"])`, against the kappa of 0.750 and overall
accuracy of 0.824 the parent study reports for its 7.78 km2 window. But
@tbl-redstage-area shows that figure is flattered by how the sample was drawn.
Training took 250 attacked and 250 unattacked cells per year, so the model's
implied prior is one half, while the survey maps attack on
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(SURV_AREA[SURV_AREA > 0]))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max(SURV_AREA))` per cent of the grid. At its own
threshold the classifier therefore calls
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(RAW_AREA))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(RAW_AREA))`
per cent of the landscape attacked, one to two orders of magnitude more ground
than the survey maps.

Matching the area does not rescue it. Calibrating the threshold each year so the
classified area equals the surveyed area, the classification lands on
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(RED_CMP$Hit, na.rm = TRUE))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(RED_CMP$Hit, na.rm = TRUE))` per cent of the cells the
survey mapped. Expressed as lift against the survey's own prevalence, where 1.00
is chance, the years run from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(RED_CMP$Lift, na.rm = TRUE))`
to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(RED_CMP$Lift, na.rm = TRUE))`, and
`r sum(RED_CMP$Lift == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of `r sum(!is.na(RED_CMP$Lift))` years
share no cells with the survey at all. Once area is held equal the map is close to
uninformative about where attack was.

The year that most exposes the mechanism is 2012. It is the only year covered by
Landsat 7 alone, whose scan line corrector has been broken since May 2003, and it
is the year the classifier calls the most attacked at
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * RAW_AREA[["2012"]])` per cent while the survey maps the
least at `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * SURV_AREA[["2012"]])` per cent. The classifier
is reading striping as change.

Two readings of the pooled agreement figure were available before these tables
existed. The classifier might have been wrong, or the polygons might have been,
and a one-sided error towards mapping more attack than an observer drew is what a
finer instrument would also produce. @tbl-redstage-area settles it against the
classifier: an instrument genuinely resolving attack the surveyor missed would
still overlap the attack the surveyor found, and this one does not. We cannot
say the survey is right, only that the classification is not measuring the same
thing.

We therefore keep the aerial overview survey as the response and report the
classification as a comparison layer. That preserves the argument the rest of the
paper rests on, which is that a response whose errors are observer errors is
safer here than one whose errors are generated by the predictors under test. A
classification trained on terrain-corrected imagery does not escape that problem,
because terrain correction is itself a model of the terrain whose effect is being
tested. It also means the timing analysis a per-cell year of first detection would
allow is not available: an annual series this weak cannot support a survival
model, and fitting one would give the wind test a precision the response layer
cannot justify.

## Host abundance

```{r}
#| label: read-host
#| echo: true

vri <- project(vect(here("02.inputs/vri/vri_darkwoods.geojson")), crs(G))
vd  <- as.data.frame(vri)
num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))

## VRI records up to three species per polygon with percentage cover
accumulate <- function(pattern) {
  out <- rep(0, nrow(vd))
  for (i in 1:3) {
    cd <- vd[[paste0("SPECIES_CD_", i)]]
    pc <- num(vd[[paste0("SPECIES_PCT_", i)]]); pc[is.na(pc)] <- 0
    out <- out + ifelse(!is.na(cd) & grepl(pattern, cd), pc, 0)
  }
  out
}
vri$PinePct <- accumulate("^PL")               # lodgepole, the primary host
vri$Basal   <- num(vd$BASAL_AREA)

## Quadratic mean diameter of stems 12.5 cm and over. Carried because stem size,
## not cover, is what decides whether a stand produces more beetles than it
## consumes: below about 25 cm a lodgepole stand is a sink, above it a source
## [@carroll2004bionomics]. Cover and basal area cannot express that.
vri$QMD <- num(vd$QUAD_DIAM_125)

host <- rast(lapply(c("PinePct","Basal","QMD"), function(f) rasterize(vri, G, field = f)))
names(host) <- c("PinePct","Basal","QMD")
c(vri_polygons = nrow(vri), with_lodgepole = sum(vri$PinePct > 0),
  with_diameter = sum(!is.na(vri$QMD)))
```

Host abundance comes from the provincial Vegetation Resources Inventory, layer `VEG_COMP_LYR_R1_POLY`, retrieved from the British Columbia Data Catalogue web feature service for the study window. We accumulate the percentage cover of lodgepole pine across the three species slots each polygon records, and carry stand basal area alongside it.

We also carry quadratic mean diameter, which the inventory records for stems 12.5 cm and over. Cover and basal area describe how much host is present. Neither describes whether that host can produce beetles. Brood production per tree rises with bark surface area, bark thickness, phloem thickness and sapwood moisture retention, and all four rise with stem diameter, so a stand of small stems consumes more beetles than it returns. Carroll and Safranyik put the crossover at about 25 cm: below it a lodgepole stand is on average a beetle sink, above it a source [@carroll2004bionomics]. That threshold is the reason a host layer coded only as cover cannot answer the question this paper asks at high elevation, and it is the gap review finding R3 identifies in the retained studies. @sec-size tests it directly. Diameter is recorded for `r format(sum(!is.na(vri$QMD)), big.mark=",")` of the `r format(nrow(vri), big.mark=",")` polygons, which covers the analysis frame almost exactly, because the polygons that lack it are largely those that also lack a basal area.

The inventory's vintage matters. These polygons carry a reference year of 2014 and an interpretation date of August 2014; the projected date of 31 December 2025 is the growth model's roll-forward of age, height and volume, not a re-observation. Species composition therefore comes from photography flown in the fourteenth year of a seventeen-year outbreak window.

This limitation cannot be removed and is stated explicitly. A stand whose pine was killed early will have been interpreted after the fact, and its recorded lodgepole percentage will be lower than the pine it carried when the beetle arrived. The bias runs in a specific direction: host is under-recorded exactly where attack was heaviest and earliest. It is therefore a candidate explanation for the reversal of the lodgepole coefficient at the severe threshold in @sec-ordinal. It does not touch the presence-absence distinction the layer is mainly used for, since a stand that carried enough pine to be killed is not recorded as pine-free.

Without this layer the analysis cannot distinguish a refugium from an absence of pine, and @sec-host shows that the distinction accounts for most of the apparent terrain signal.

@fig-host maps both layers. Lodgepole cover is concentrated in the middle of the elevation range and scarce in the valley, which is the pattern the host-conditioning argument turns on: the valley is not lightly attacked because it is sheltered but because it holds almost no host. Basal area defines the analysis frame, and the blank cells in panel (b) are those dropped for want of it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-host
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "The forest inventory host layers, rasterised onto the analysis grid. (a) Lodgepole pine cover, accumulated across the three species slots each polygon records. (b) Stand basal area, which defines the analysis frame: cells with no recorded basal area are dropped. Unshaded ground is unmapped or non-productive. Projection and scale as in @fig-site."

fig_host <-
  (ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = host$PinePct) +
     scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                          name = "Lodgepole\ncover (%)") +
     clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(a) Lodgepole pine cover", subtitle = sub_utm)) |
  (ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = host$Basal) +
     scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                          name = "Basal area\n(m² ha⁻¹)") +
     clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(b) Stand basal area", subtitle = sub_utm))
fig_host
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-host-maps.png", fig_host,
       width = 180, height = 96, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

## Terrain and wind

```{r}
#| label: read-terrain
#| echo: true

to_grid <- function(f) {
  r <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", f))
  b <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), crs(r))
  project(crop(r, b, snap = "out"), G, method = "bilinear")
}
terr <- rast(list(Elevation = G,               Slope = to_grid("Slope.utm.tif"),
                  TWI       = to_grid("TWI.utm.tif"),
                  RIX       = to_grid("Rutm.tif"),
                  Wind      = to_grid("Wind.utm.tif")))
names(terr) <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind")

## Topographic position: mean deviation from a surrounding annulus.
tpi <- function(r, w) {
  k <- matrix(1, w, w); k[ceiling(w/2), ceiling(w/2)] <- 0
  r - focal(r, k / sum(k), fun = sum, na.policy = "omit", na.rm = TRUE)
}
terr$TPI600 <- tpi(G, 25)     # ~625 m neighbourhood
```

```{r}
#| label: aspect-terms
#| echo: true

## Two surfaces built from aspect, which the inherited set lacks entirely.
## Both are computed directly from the elevation model rather than draped over
## it, which is why @tbl-orthogonality can show them independent of elevation.
d2r <- pi / 180
asp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Aspect.utm.tif"))
slp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Slope.utm.tif"))
stopifnot(identical(dim(asp), dim(G)), identical(as.vector(ext(asp)), as.vector(ext(G))))

## Heat load after McCune and Keon, aspect folded about the SW-NE axis so that
## southwest is hottest. Flat cells carry a -1 sentinel; the sin(slope) factor
## nulls the aspect term there, so the substitution below is inert.
asp[asp < 0] <- 225
fold <- abs(180 - abs(asp - 225))
LAT  <- mean(crds(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:4326"))[, 2])
terr$HLI <- 0.339 + 0.808 * cos(LAT*d2r) * cos(slp*d2r) -
            0.196 * sin(LAT*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r) -
            0.482 * cos(fold*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r)

## Winstral shelter index: the maximum upwind slope angle within SEARCH metres
## along a bearing. Positive means terrain rises upwind, so the cell is
## sheltered; negative means it is exposed. The Global Wind Atlas gives speed
## but no direction, so rather than assume a prevailing bearing we compute all
## eight and average, giving an omnidirectional shelter index.
SEARCH <- 500
shift_mat <- function(m, dr, dc) {
  nr <- nrow(m); nc <- ncol(m); out <- matrix(NA_real_, nr, nc)
  ri <- seq_len(nr); ci <- seq_len(nc); sr <- ri + dr; sc <- ci + dc
  vr <- sr >= 1 & sr <= nr; vc <- sc >= 1 & sc <= nc
  out[ri[vr], ci[vc]] <- m[sr[vr], sc[vc]]
  out
}
zm <- as.matrix(G, wide = TRUE); rstep <- res(G)[1]
sx_dir <- function(az) {
  th <- az * d2r; best <- matrix(-Inf, nrow(zm), ncol(zm))
  for (k in 1:floor(SEARCH / rstep)) {
    dc <- round(k * sin(th)); dr <- round(-k * cos(th))
    if (dc == 0 && dr == 0) next
    best <- pmax(best, atan((shift_mat(zm, dr, dc) - zm) / (k * rstep)) / d2r, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  best[!is.finite(best)] <- NA_real_
  best
}
sx <- rast(lapply(seq(0, 315, by = 45), function(a) {
  r <- G; values(r) <- as.vector(t(sx_dir(a))); r }))
terr$SxMean <- app(sx, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Terrain surfaces are inherited unchanged from @murphy2026, which derived them from the 1 m Natural Resources Canada High Resolution Digital Elevation Model [@nrcan2017], smoothed, depression-filled by the algorithm of @wang2006 and aggregated to 25 m, with compound indices following @beers1973 and @parker1982. We add three surfaces of our own. The first is a topographic position index at a 625 m neighbourhood, because @cartwright2018 found slope, elevation and heat load among the strongest controls on refugia and reported topographic position alongside them, and the inherited set carried none.

The other two exist because the inherited set carries no aspect information, and so no term that can distinguish a warm slope from a cold one at the same elevation. That matters because the confound this paper cannot resolve is between wind exposure and cold, and aspect bears on the two differently. We compute a heat load index after @mccune2002, in which aspect is folded about the southwest to northeast axis so that southwest is hottest, and a shelter index after @winstral2002, the maximum upwind slope angle within 500 m along a bearing, positive where terrain rises upwind and negative on exposed convexities. The Global Wind Atlas supplies speed but no direction, so rather than assume a prevailing bearing we compute the index on all eight cardinal and intercardinal bearings and average them.

The decisive property of both is how they are built. They are derived from the elevation model by trigonometry rather than draped over it by downscaling, and @tbl-orthogonality shows the consequence: their variance is essentially unrelated to elevation, where the wind product's is largely elevation. A terrain-derived predictor is not automatically an elevation transform; the distinction is in the construction.

The ruggedness surface carries a documentation gap we state rather than paper over. Its exact formulation is not recorded beyond the citations above, and its distribution is inconsistent with a vector ruggedness measure. We treat it as a reproducible but unnamed ruggedness surface and confine claims to its statistical behaviour.

Ambient wind is Global Wind Atlas mean wind speed at 10 m above ground level [@globalwindatlas]. The atlas is built by driving a mesoscale model from reanalysis, generalising the result by the method of @badger2014 to remove the local terrain and roughness signal, then downscaling it over a digital elevation model and a land-cover roughness map [@davis2023]. Elevation and roughness are inputs to the product, not covariates measured independently of it. That is why it cannot be assumed independent of elevation, and testing that assumption is the second half of this paper.

Figure S1 maps the six derived surfaces. Their point is visual rather than statistical: slope, wetness, ruggedness and topographic position all trace the same drainage network and valley wall, whereas heat load and the shelter index divide the landscape by aspect, picking out southwest-facing ground the others do not distinguish. That is the difference @tbl-orthogonality quantifies.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 4.6

fig_terrain <-
  (panel(terr$Slope,  "(a) Slope", "Degrees", "cividis") |
   panel(terr$TWI,    "(b) Topographic wetness index", "TWI", "mako", -1) |
   panel(terr$RIX,    "(c) Ruggedness", "Index", "rocket", -1)) /
  (panel(terr$TPI600, "(d) Topographic position, 625 m", "TPI (m)", "viridis") |
   panel(terr$HLI,    "(e) Heat load index", "HLI", "inferno") |
   panel(terr$SxMean, "(f) Shelter index, omnidirectional", "Sx (deg)", "cividis", -1))
fig_terrain
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-terrain-maps.png", fig_terrain,
       width = 180, height = 118, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

## Climate records

Because the interpretation in @sec-krawchuk turns on whether it is cold enough at the top of the gradient to kill beetles, we assembled the observational record. Hourly observations from the British Columbia Wildfire Service network and daily observations from Environment and Climate Change Canada were retrieved for all stations within 100 km for the winters of the outbreak window. The script in `02.inputs/climate/` streams roughly 2.7 GB and writes the per-station-winter summary the manuscript reads. That division is deliberate: the fetch cannot sit inside a document render, but every decision about which records to believe is made in @sec-cold, in code, and is visible there.

Two screens matter. Many older Wildfire Service sensors floor at exactly -20.0 °C, so a station-winter whose minimum sits on that floor has an unknown true minimum and is excluded; the rule is applied and checked in @sec-cold rather than inherited. Isolated spikes, colder than both neighbouring observations by more than 15 °C, are rejected as instrument error at the observation level, the one screen that must happen during retrieval because it needs the sub-daily series. One such value, a -40.0 °C daily minimum on a day whose maximum was -4.5 °C and carrying no quality flag, would otherwise have produced exactly the conclusion the record does not support.

A second script in the same directory, `add-minimum-dates.R`, reads the winter extracts the fetch already cached and records the date on which each station-winter reached its minimum. It runs outside the render for the same reason, and its output is small and is kept with the manuscript. The date is needed because lethal temperature for this insect is conditional on the state of cold-hardening rather than fixed, so a minimum without a date cannot be compared with a lethal range.

The window is December to February, which is what the question about deep-winter minima required. That choice bounds what the record can support, and @sec-cold states the bound rather than working around it. This network cannot furnish a temperature surface. It can establish whether deep-winter air temperature in this region approaches the lethal range, a weaker and, for one purpose, sufficient claim.

```{r}
#| label: assemble
#| echo: true

clip_src <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Oubteak.2005.tif"))
in_clip  <- rasterize(project(as.polygons(ext(clip_src), crs = crs(clip_src)), crs(G)),
                      G, field = 1, background = 0)

X <- as.data.frame(c(terr, host, severity, in_clip), na.rm = FALSE)
names(X)[(ncol(X) - 1):ncol(X)] <- c("Severity","InClip")
X$Attacked <- X$Severity > 0
X$HasHost  <- !is.na(X$PinePct) & X$PinePct > 0

## spatial blocks for resampling-based inference
rc <- rowColFromCell(G, seq_len(ncell(G)))
X$block <- paste(rc[,1] %/% BLOCK, rc[,2] %/% BLOCK, sep = "_")

PRED  <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind","TPI600")
EXTRA <- c("HLI","SxMean")          # aspect-derived; enter only the extended model
MVARS <- c(PRED, "PinePct", "Basal")   # defines the analysis frame, deliberately unchanged

## Cells lacking an inventory basal area are unmapped or non-productive and cannot
## enter a model that conditions on stand structure. Dropping them is reported here
## rather than left to silent na.action inside glm.
n_before <- sum(complete.cases(X[, PRED]) & !is.na(X$PinePct))
S <- X[complete.cases(X[, MVARS]), ]
H <- S[S$HasHost, ]
c(with_terrain_and_host = n_before, dropped_no_basal_area = n_before - nrow(S),
  analysis_cells = nrow(S), km2 = round(nrow(S) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6, 1),
  attacked = sum(S$Attacked), host_cells = nrow(H))
```
