```{r}
#| label: tbl-relief
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The analysis landscape, and the 2 by 4 km clip drawn from it that the companion study used. The clip samples under two thirds of the relief and under 4 per cent of the cells."

tibble(
  Extent = c("full landscape", "2 by 4 km clip"),
  Cells  = c(nrow(S), sum(S$InClip == 1)),
  `Area (km²)` = round(c(nrow(S), sum(S$InClip == 1)) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6, 1),
  `Elevation (m)` = c(sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(S$Elevation), max(S$Elevation)),
                      sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1]),
                                              max(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1]))),
  `Relief (m)` = round(c(diff(range(S$Elevation)), diff(range(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1])))),
  `Attacked (%)` = round(100 * c(mean(S$Attacked), mean(S$Attacked[S$InClip==1])), 1)
) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

# Methods

## Inference

The response is heavily clustered, so cell counts vastly overstate independent information. All coefficients carry percentile intervals from a spatial block bootstrap, meaning the landscape is cut into square tiles and whole tiles are drawn at random with replacement, so neighbouring cells travel together and are never treated as separate evidence. The landscape is partitioned into blocks of `r BLOCK` by `r BLOCK` cells, roughly 1 km on a side, resampled with replacement `r B_BOOT` times. Blocks of this size exceed any plausible correlation range of the survey polygons. We report the point estimate, the block interval and the proportion of resamples reproducing its sign, and treat a term as supported only when the interval excludes zero.

```{r}
#| label: fn-boot
#| echo: true

## The bootstrap refits several hundred times on >100,000 rows, so it works on a
## model matrix built once and calls glm.fit directly. This is arithmetically
## identical to glm() with the same formula, and roughly thirty times faster.
MODEL_VARS <- c("Elevation","WindResid","PinePct","Basal","TPI600","Slope","TWI","RIX")

design_matrix <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS)
  cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, as.matrix(z[, vars, drop = FALSE]))

fit_fast <- function(Xm, y) glm.fit(Xm, y, family = binomial())

## The resamples are drawn first, in one sequence from one seed, and only then
## fitted. That ordering is the whole point: the random number stream is consumed
## in exactly the order the original serial loop consumed it, so every interval in
## this paper is bit-identical to the serial implementation, and the fitting, which
## is the expensive part, can be spread across cores. Seeding inside each worker
## instead would be simpler and would change every reported interval.
##
## Measured on the analysis frame: the matrix subsetting costs about 2 per cent of
## a replicate and glm.fit about 98, so there is nothing to gain from cleverer
## indexing, and two attempts at it were slower than the original. Four cores gives
## about 1.7 times; eight is slower again on this machine, which has four
## performance cores.
BOOT_CORES <- max(1L, min(4L, parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) - 1L))

block_boot <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS, B = B_BOOT, seed = 42) {
  Xm <- design_matrix(z, vars); y <- z$y
  idx_of <- split(seq_len(nrow(z)), z$block)
  blocks <- names(idx_of)
  set.seed(seed)
  draws <- lapply(seq_len(B), function(b) sample(blocks, length(blocks), replace = TRUE))
  one <- function(k) {
    idx <- unlist(idx_of[k], use.names = FALSE)
    f <- try(fit_fast(Xm[idx, , drop = FALSE], y[idx]), silent = TRUE)
    if (inherits(f, "try-error")) rep(NA_real_, ncol(Xm)) else coef(f)
  }
  ## mclapply forks, which is unavailable on Windows; fall back rather than fail.
  res <- if (BOOT_CORES > 1L && .Platform$OS.type == "unix")
           parallel::mclapply(draws, one, mc.cores = BOOT_CORES) else lapply(draws, one)
  matrix(unlist(res), B, ncol(Xm), byrow = TRUE,
         dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Xm)))
}

model_table <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS, seed = 42) {
  Xm <- design_matrix(z, vars)
  fit <- fit_fast(Xm, z$y)
  cf  <- coef(fit)
  se  <- sqrt(diag(chol2inv(fit$qr$qr[1:fit$rank, 1:fit$rank, drop = FALSE])))
  bs  <- block_boot(z, vars, seed = seed)
  tibble(term = names(cf), beta = as.numeric(cf), naive_z = as.numeric(cf / se),
         lo = apply(bs, 2, quantile, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
         hi = apply(bs, 2, quantile, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
         sign_stab = sapply(names(cf), function(n)
                       mean(sign(bs[, n]) == sign(cf[n]), na.rm = TRUE)))
}

fmt_model <- function(mt) {
  mt |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    transmute(Term = term, beta = sprintf("%+.3f", beta),
              `naive z` = sprintf("%+.1f", naive_z),
              `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", lo, hi),
              `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f", sign_stab),
              Supported = ifelse(lo * hi > 0, "yes", "no"))
}
```

## Orthogonalisation

Review finding R5 is the reason this step exists. Because the wind surface is built over the elevation surface, its coefficient in a model containing elevation is estimated from whatever small part of the joint distribution lets the two vary separately. We therefore replace wind by the residual of wind regressed on elevation, rescaled to unit variance. Orthogonalisation here means exactly that: keep only the part of the wind surface that a straight line in elevation cannot predict.

The substitution is sometimes presented as a remedy for collinearity, which it is not. The substitution is a linear reparameterisation of the same model: fitted values and deviance are unchanged, and by the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem the residualised coefficient is the raw wind coefficient multiplied by the square root of one minus the R² of wind on elevation, with its standard error scaled identically. Every supported-or-not verdict in this paper is therefore numerically the same in both parameterisations, and orthogonalisation buys no precision whatever. What changes is interpretation. The wind coefficient now refers to the part of the wind surface elevation does not explain, which is the quantity the @krawchuk2020 hypothesis is about, and the elevation coefficient becomes the total elevation association rather than the partial effect at fixed wind. The reparameterisation is therefore justified on interpretative grounds alone.

```{r}
#| label: design
#| echo: true

standardise <- function(dd) {
  vars <- intersect(c(PRED, EXTRA, "PinePct", "Basal"), names(dd))
  z <- as.data.frame(scale(dd[, vars]))
  z$y     <- as.integer(dd$Attacked)
  z$block <- dd$block
  z$Severity <- dd$Severity          # carried for the ordinal fits in @sec-ordinal
  z$WindResid <- as.numeric(scale(residuals(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))))
  z
}
Z  <- standardise(S)     # whole landscape
ZH <- standardise(H)     # cells containing lodgepole
ZC <- standardise(S[S$InClip == 1, ])   # the 2 by 4 km clip
round(cor(Z[, c("Elevation","Wind","WindResid")]), 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-orthogonality
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "How much of each candidate predictor is elevation. The wind product is a mesoscale field draped over terrain and is largely an elevation transform. The heat load and shelter indices are computed from the same elevation model by trigonometry and are almost unrelated to it."

tibble(Surface = c("Global Wind Atlas wind speed", "Heat load index (McCune and Keon)",
                   "Shelter index (Winstral, omnidirectional)", "Topographic position, 625 m"),
       `How it is built` = c("mesoscale field downscaled over the DEM",
                             "trigonometric function of DEM aspect and slope",
                             "maximum upwind slope from the DEM within 500 m",
                             "deviation from surrounding DEM mean"),
       `R² on elevation` = sapply(c("Wind","HLI","SxMean","TPI600"), function(v)
         round(summary(lm(as.formula(paste(v, "~ Elevation")), data = Z))$r.squared, 3))) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lll")
```

## Response specification

@krawchuk2020 warn against coding refugia as a binary, since a refugium is a matter of degree and thresholding discards the signal distinguishing a lightly touched stand from a destroyed one. The survey carries an ordinal severity class, so we can follow that advice. We fit the binary attacked model for comparability with the refugia literature, and alongside it a cumulative logit at each severity threshold. A cumulative logit asks a yes-or-no question at each cut in turn: attacked at all or not, moderate or worse or not, and so on.

Fitting those thresholds separately, rather than imposing one slope across all of them, is deliberate. The single-slope version assumes proportional odds, meaning a predictor pushes a stand up every step of the severity scale by the same amount. Comparing the separate fits is the standard diagnostic for whether that assumption holds, and @sec-ordinal shows that here it does not.

# Results

## Elevational distribution {#sec-host}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gradient
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Attack across the elevation gradient, before and after conditioning on lodgepole presence. Conditioning flattens the gradient below 1,900 m but not above it, where attack halves while lodgepole cover rises and stands thin."

S$band <- cut(S$Elevation, breaks = seq(500, 2400, 200), dig.lab = 5)
grad <- S |> group_by(band) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(),
            `Pine cover (%)` = round(mean(PinePct), 1),
            `Basal area` = round(mean(Basal, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            `Wind (m/s)` = round(mean(Wind), 2),
            `Attacked, all cells (%)` = round(100 * mean(Attacked), 1),
            `Attacked, host present (%)` =
              ifelse(sum(HasHost) > 300, round(100 * mean(Attacked[HasHost]), 1), NA),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(Cells > 500)
grad |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

## Spread of host-conditioned attack below 1,900 m, quoted in the text below.
hp_low <- S |> filter(HasHost, Elevation < 1900) |>
  mutate(b = cut(Elevation, seq(500, 1900, 200))) |>
  group_by(b) |> summarise(n = n(), pct = 100 * mean(Attacked), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n > 300)
HP_RANGE <- range(hp_low$pct)

## Host cover above the threshold, compared two ways, because the two
## comparisons disagree and reporting only the flattering one would be the
## same denominator problem examined in @sec-lowtrap. PINE_LO is
## the whole gradient below the threshold, which is dominated by the pine-poor
## valley; PINE_ADJ is the 150 m band immediately below it.
PINE_HI  <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation >= ALPINE])
PINE_LO  <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation <  ALPINE])
PINE_ADJ <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation >= ALPINE - 150 & H$Elevation < ALPINE])
```

Across the full gradient attack is strongly unimodal (@tbl-gradient, @fig-gradient), rising from under three per cent in the valley to a peak near 1,430 m and falling to zero above 2,100 m.

Conditioning on host presence separates that curve into two phenomena. Below roughly 1,900 m the hump is host distribution: among cells containing lodgepole, attack runs between `r sprintf("%.0f", HP_RANGE[1])` and `r sprintf("%.0f", HP_RANGE[2])` per cent with no strong trend from the valley bottom upward, and the rise in the raw curve is the rise in pine cover. Attack is `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(S$Attacked[S$HasHost]))` per cent where lodgepole is present against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(S$Attacked[!S$HasHost]))` per cent where it is absent.

Above `r format(ALPINE, big.mark = ",")` m conditioning does not remove the decline. Attack among host-bearing cells falls by about half, while stand basal area falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(H$Basal[H$Elevation<ALPINE], na.rm=TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(H$Basal[H$Elevation>=ALPINE], na.rm=TRUE))`. Stands are thinner and attack is suppressed.

Whether this is the pattern the @krawchuk2020 hypothesis requires depends on host cover, and on which comparison is made, so both are reported. Against the whole gradient below, mean lodgepole cover in host-bearing cells is `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_HI)` per cent above the threshold against `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_LO)` per cent below: essentially unchanged, so host scarcity cannot account for an attack rate that more than halves. Against the `r format(ALPINE - 150, big.mark = ",")` to `r format(ALPINE, big.mark = ",")` m band immediately below, however, cover is `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_ADJ)` per cent, so the top of the gradient carries about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - PINE_HI / PINE_ADJ))` per cent less pine than the band beneath it. The first comparison is inflated by the pine-poor valley it includes, which is the denominator problem examined in @sec-lowtrap, and it is not relied on alone.

The honest reading is that host thins somewhat at the top while attack falls a great deal more, so the conjunction the hypothesis requires holds in the weaker form. It is not the clean case of host holding constant.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gradient
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "(a) Attack across the gradient, raw and conditioned on lodgepole presence, with mean lodgepole cover. (b) The same data against wind speed: wind rises monotonically with elevation while attack turns over, so no monotone wind relationship can hold across the gradient. Shading marks the elevation range of the 2 by 4 km clip."

fine <- S |> mutate(b = cut(Elevation, breaks = seq(500, 2350, 100))) |>
  group_by(b) |>
  summarise(el = mean(Elevation), raw = 100*mean(Attacked), pine = mean(PinePct),
            wind = mean(Wind), n = n(),
            cond = ifelse(sum(HasHost) > 150, 100*mean(Attacked[HasHost]), NA_real_),
            .groups = "drop") |> filter(n > 300)
crng <- range(S$Elevation[S$InClip == 1])

pa <- ggplot(fine) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = crng[1], xmax = crng[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#b2182b", alpha = .10) +
  geom_line(aes(el, raw,  colour = "all cells"), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_line(aes(el, cond, colour = "host present"), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_line(aes(el, pine, colour = "lodgepole cover (%)"), linetype = "22", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("all cells" = "#2b4162", "host present" = "#b2182b",
                                 "lodgepole cover (%)" = "#3f8f9b"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Per cent", title = "(a) Attack and lodgepole cover against elevation") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

pb <- ggplot(fine, aes(wind, raw)) +
  geom_path(colour = "#3f8f9b", linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = el), size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours = c("#2b4162","#3f8f9b","#c6d8af","#e8c07d","#8c4b3c"),
                         name = "Elev (m)") +
  labs(x = "Mean wind speed (m/s)", y = "Attacked (%)",
       title = "(b) Attack against mean wind speed")
pa + pb
```

## Stem diameter effects {#sec-size}

The result above rests on lodgepole cover holding while attack halves. Cover is the wrong host variable to rest it on. What decides whether a stand returns more beetles than it consumes is stem diameter, and the published crossover is about 25 cm [@carroll2004bionomics]. A subalpine stand and a montane stand can carry identical cover and identical basal area while differing entirely in stem size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-size
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Attack by stand quadratic mean diameter, in cells carrying lodgepole pine. The published source-sink crossover for lodgepole is about 25 cm [@carroll2004bionomics]. The observed distribution reproduces that threshold without it being imposed."

HQ <- H[!is.na(H$QMD), ]
HQ$dclass <- cut(HQ$QMD, c(0, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, Inf),
                 labels = c("≤ 15", "15 to 20", "20 to 25",
                            "25 to 30", "30 to 35", "> 35"))

HQ |> group_by(`Quadratic mean diameter (cm)` = dclass) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(), `Attacked (%)` = round(100*mean(Attacked), 1),
            `Lodgepole cover (%)` = round(mean(PinePct), 1),
            `Basal area (m² ha⁻¹)` = round(mean(Basal), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Attack rises monotonically with stem size, from `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$QMD <= 15]))` per cent in the smallest class to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$QMD > 35]))` per cent in the largest. The steepest step falls at the 25 cm boundary the entomology names. Cover does not order the same way, and in the largest diameter class it is at its lowest, so this is not cover under another name.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-size-elev
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The high-elevation decline, decomposed. Host cover is flat across the threshold; stem size is not. The final column restricts to stands above the 25 cm source-sink crossover, where the decline persists."

sz <- function(d) tibble(
  Cells = nrow(d),
  `Attacked (%)`         = round(100*mean(d$Attacked), 1),
  `Lodgepole cover (%)`  = round(mean(d$PinePct), 1),
  `Basal area (m² ha⁻¹)` = round(mean(d$Basal), 1),
  `Mean diameter (cm)`   = round(mean(d$QMD), 1),
  `Stands > 25 cm (%)`   = round(100*mean(d$QMD > 25), 1),
  `Attacked, > 25 cm only (%)` = round(100*mean(d$Attacked[d$QMD > 25]), 1))

bind_rows(sz(HQ[HQ$Elevation <  ALPINE, ]), sz(HQ[HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE, ])) |>
  mutate(Band = c(sprintf("below %s m", format(ALPINE, big.mark=",")),
                  sprintf("above %s m", format(ALPINE, big.mark=","))), .before = 1) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: size-conditioning
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## How much of the high-elevation suppression is stem size? Fit the same
## indicator three ways and read the attenuation. Nested fits on one frame, so
## the coefficients are directly comparable.
HQ$Hi <- HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE
hi_alone <- coef(glm(Attacked ~ Hi, HQ, family = binomial))[["HiTRUE"]]
hi_qmd   <- coef(glm(Attacked ~ Hi + QMD, HQ, family = binomial))[["HiTRUE"]]
hi_full  <- coef(glm(Attacked ~ Hi + QMD + PinePct + Basal,
                     HQ, family = binomial))[["HiTRUE"]]
```

Mean quadratic diameter falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(HQ$QMD[HQ$Elevation < ALPINE]))` cm below the threshold to `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(HQ$QMD[HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE]))` cm above it, and the share of stands above the source-sink crossover falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$QMD[HQ$Elevation < ALPINE] > 25))` per cent to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$QMD[HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE] > 25))` per cent. Cover over the same step moves from `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(HQ$PinePct[HQ$Elevation < ALPINE]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(HQ$PinePct[HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE]))` per cent. So part of the suppression we attributed to a non-host mechanism is host quality, and reporting cover alone concealed it.

The claim survives the correction. Within source stands only, those above 25 cm, attack still falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$Elevation < ALPINE & HQ$QMD > 25]))` per cent to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$Elevation >= ALPINE & HQ$QMD > 25]))` per cent across the threshold. Fitted as a single indicator the log-odds of attack above `r format(ALPINE, big.mark=",")` m is `r sprintf("%+.3f", hi_alone)`; adding diameter leaves `r sprintf("%+.3f", hi_qmd)`, and adding cover and basal area alongside it leaves `r sprintf("%+.3f", hi_full)`. Stem size absorbs about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1 - hi_qmd/hi_alone))` per cent of the effect and the full host set about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1 - hi_full/hi_alone))` per cent. The remaining `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*hi_full/hi_alone)` per cent is not host in any coding.

That is the version of the high-elevation result we defend. It is weaker than the one cover alone implies and it rests on the host variable the entomology says governs brood production.

## Wind disruption test {#sec-krawchuk}

This is the first fit of the term review finding R1 identified as proposed but never entered: the component of the wind surface independent of elevation, in cells carrying host.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

mt_h <- model_table(ZH)
SUPP_KRAWCHUK <- fmt_model(mt_h) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllll")
```

```{r}
#| label: krawchuk-numbers
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| output: false
wr <- mt_h[mt_h$term == "WindResid", ]
pp <- mt_h[mt_h$term == "PinePct", ]
```

Restricted to cells containing host, the orthogonalised wind term is the largest negative coefficient in the model, `r sprintf("%+.3f", wr$beta)` per standard deviation, comparable to the positive effect of lodgepole cover at `r sprintf("%+.3f", pp$beta)` (Table S1). Its sign is reproduced in `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*wr$sign_stab)` per cent of block resamples, but its 95 per cent block interval runs `r sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", wr$lo, wr$hi)` and reaches zero.

On this fit the hypothesis is supported in direction and unresolved in magnitude, and @sec-nonlinear later withdraws even the direction, so read this section as the conventional analysis whose specification we go on to test rather than a result we stand behind. The descriptive result in @sec-host is not in doubt: attack more than halves at the top of the gradient while host cover thins only slightly. What is in doubt is whether wind is the right explanation, and with roughly `r length(unique(ZH$block))` independent 1 km blocks the binary response cannot settle it. Host cover is the only term whose interval excludes zero.

That verdict is a property of the response coding rather than of the data, and @sec-ordinal revisits it. We report the binary model first because it is the form the refugia literature uses, and the comparison is itself a result.

Elevation, entered alongside the orthogonalised wind term, is itself negative and unsupported: once host is in the model the remaining elevation signal is weak, so the suppression at the top is not simply an elevation effect.

## Ordinal severity models {#sec-ordinal}

```{r}
#| label: polr-fit
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Fitted only to show what a single proportional-odds summary conceals; the
## threshold-specific fits in @tbl-ordinal are the result.
zo <- ZH; zo$sev <- factor(pmin(zo$Severity, 4L), levels = 0:4, ordered = TRUE)
polr_fit <- MASS::polr(sev ~ Elevation + WindResid + PinePct + Basal +
                             TPI600 + Slope + TWI + RIX,
                       data = zo, method = "logistic", Hess = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ordinal
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Cumulative logits at each severity threshold, cells containing lodgepole pine only. The orthogonalised wind coefficient strengthens monotonically as the threshold rises and its block interval excludes zero above trace, which the binary model does not show."

CUTS <- tibble(k = 1:4,
               label = c("trace or worse", "light or worse",
                         "moderate or worse", "severe or worse"))

cum <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(CUTS)), function(i) {
  z <- ZH; z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= CUTS$k[i])
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y)
  bs  <- block_boot(z)
  q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Threshold = CUTS$label[i], Cells = sum(z$y),
         `Wind residual beta` = coef(fit)[["WindResid"]],
         lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
         `sign stability` = mean(sign(bs[, "WindResid"]) ==
                                 sign(coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]), na.rm = TRUE),
         `Pine cover beta` = coef(fit)[["PinePct"]],
         `Elevation beta`  = coef(fit)[["Elevation"]])
}) |> bind_rows()

cum |> transmute(Threshold, Cells,
                 `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", `Wind residual beta`),
                 `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", lo, hi),
                 `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f", `sign stability`),
                 `Pine cover beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", `Pine cover beta`),
                 Supported = ifelse(lo * hi > 0, "yes", "no")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Collapsing the response to attacked or not costs the study its main result. Fitted at successively harder severity thresholds, the orthogonalised wind coefficient strengthens monotonically from `r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])` at trace or worse to `r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4])` at severe or worse, a `r sprintf("%.1f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4] / cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])`-fold increase (@tbl-ordinal). At every threshold above trace the block interval excludes zero. The first row is the binary model of @sec-krawchuk restated, since a cell reaching trace or worse is exactly a cell recorded as attacked, so the table extends that fit rather than competing with it. It is also the weakest of the four, and the one the refugia literature would conventionally have reported.

This is a dose-response gradient of the shape the hypothesis predicts. Wherever the wind surface has a component independent of elevation, that component is associated with less attack, and the association is strongest where attack was heaviest. It also explains the binary result: a cell that reached trace severity is barely distinguishable from an unattacked cell, so a threshold drawn between them puts most of the noise exactly where the model is asked to fit.

The slopes differ by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4] / cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])` across the thresholds, so proportional odds does not hold and a single ordinal coefficient would be the wrong summary. Fitting one anyway returns `r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(polr_fit)[["WindResid"]])`, close to the trace-threshold estimate and concealing everything above it. Two other terms move with the threshold. Lodgepole cover, the only term that cleared the interval test in the binary model, weakens as the threshold rises and reverses at severe or worse (`r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Pine cover beta"[4])`). One reading is ecological: host abundance governs whether a stand is attacked at all, not how hard. A second is an artefact of the inventory's vintage, and we cannot separate them. Composition was interpreted from 2014 photography, late in the outbreak window, so stands that lost their pine early carry a lower recorded lodgepole percentage than when the beetle reached them. That predicts a negative coefficient at the heaviest severities, which is what is observed. We report the reversal and decline to interpret it. Elevation turns positive at moderate or worse (`r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Elevation beta"[3])`), consistent with severe attack having concentrated in the mid-elevation pine belt rather than at either end.

We cannot attribute the gradient to wind rather than cold, and the Discussion explains why the ordinal result does not help. More seriously, @sec-nonlinear shows the sweep does not survive entering elevation flexibly, so what looks here like improved support is largely the unimodal elevation response returning through a predictor orthogonalised only against the linear part of elevation. Read this table together with that one.

## Nonlinear elevation specification {#sec-nonlinear}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nonlinear
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The ordinal sweep refitted with elevation entered flexibly instead of linearly, and wind residualised against that same basis. Elevation explains eleven points more of the wind surface once curvature is allowed, and no threshold clears the interval test under either flexible basis."

## Everything above enters elevation as one linear term, and orthogonalises wind
## against that same straight line. But @fig-gradient shows the response is
## unimodal in elevation, and a straight line through a hump leaves a structured,
## elevation-shaped residual that any covariate correlated with the curvature can
## absorb. The wind surface is such a covariate by construction, because the
## downscaling is a nonlinear function of terrain. Residualising against a line
## cannot remove curvature the line never described. This table tests that.

elev_basis <- function(E, basis) switch(basis,
  linear = cbind(ElevL = E),
  quad   = cbind(ElevL = E, ElevQ = E^2),
  spline = { b <- splines::ns(E, df = 4); colnames(b) <- paste0("ElevS", 1:4); as.matrix(b) })

nl_row <- function(basis) {
  z  <- ZH
  EB <- elev_basis(z$Elevation, basis)
  z  <- cbind(z[, setdiff(names(z), "Elevation")], as.data.frame(EB))
  ## wind residualised on THIS basis, not on the straight line
  z$WindResid <- as.numeric(scale(residuals(lm(z$Wind ~ EB))))
  vars <- c(colnames(EB), "WindResid", "PinePct", "Basal", "TPI600", "Slope", "TWI", "RIX")
  r2 <- summary(lm(z$Wind ~ EB))$r.squared
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(CUTS)), function(i) {
    z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= CUTS$k[i])
    fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, vars), z$y)
    bs  <- block_boot(z, vars)
    q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
    tibble(`Elevation basis` = basis, `R² wind on basis` = round(r2, 3),
           Threshold = CUTS$label[i],
           `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]),
           `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2]),
           Supported = ifelse(q[1]*q[2] > 0, "yes", "no"))
  }) |> bind_rows()
}
nl <- bind_rows(lapply(c("linear","quad","spline"), nl_row))
nl |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllll")
```

@sandel2015 gives the diagnostic that motivates this test. For a genuinely linear relationship a coefficient is extent-independent and only the coefficient of determination moves as extent changes; a coefficient that changes sign under truncation is a symptom of an unmodelled nonlinearity rather than a general law of extent. Our response is unimodal in elevation and our wind surface monotone in it, exactly the configuration that produces such a symptom, so the specification has to be tested rather than assumed.

It does not pass. Entering elevation as a quadratic raises the share of the wind surface that elevation explains from `r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(nl$"R² wind on basis"[1]))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(nl$"R² wind on basis"[5]))`, and a natural spline on four degrees of freedom raises it to `r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(nl$"R² wind on basis"[9]))`. Roughly eleven percentage points of the wind surface's variance is therefore nonlinear in elevation, and the linear orthogonalisation used above leaves all of it inside what we had been calling the component of wind independent of elevation.

When that residue is removed the wind result goes with it. The coefficient at severe or worse falls from `r nl$"Wind residual beta"[4]` to `r nl$"Wind residual beta"[8]`, and at moderate or worse from `r nl$"Wind residual beta"[3]` to `r nl$"Wind residual beta"[7]`, losing between three fifths and seven tenths of its magnitude. Under both flexible bases every interval covers zero at every threshold. The monotone strengthening across thresholds survives in the point estimates, but nothing in the sweep clears the test this paper set itself.

We report this as the result rather than relegating it to a sensitivity appendix, because it changes what the preceding two sections mean. The dose-response in @tbl-ordinal is not evidence about wind. It is very largely the unimodal elevation response reappearing through a predictor that was never orthogonal to the curvature of elevation, only to its slope. This study does not have a wind effect to report, and the appearance of one followed from how elevation was specified.

## Aspect-derived predictors {#sec-aspect}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-aspect
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The host-present model with the two aspect-derived terms added, at each threshold it can carry. Heat load is positive and strengthens sharply with severity: warmer aspects burn harder at the same elevation. The orthogonalised wind term is not displaced by it. The shelter index carries the opposite sign, and this result is examined rather than set aside."

FULLV <- c(MODEL_VARS, EXTRA)
ZHx   <- ZH[complete.cases(ZH[, FULLV]), ]

## Ten terms and 1,522 events cannot be fitted together: the severe threshold
## drives fitted probabilities to numerical zero. We detect that rather than
## report the resulting coefficients, and the severe row is dropped below.
sep_check <- function(z, vars, k) {
  z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= k)
  p <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, vars), z$y)$fitted.values
  sum(p < 1e-6 | p > 1 - 1e-6)
}
sep <- sapply(1:4, function(k) sep_check(ZHx, FULLV, k))
names(sep) <- c("trace+","light+","moderate+","severe+")
OK_CUTS <- which(sep == 0)

asp_tab <- lapply(OK_CUTS, function(k) {
  z <- ZHx; z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= k)
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, FULLV), z$y); bs <- block_boot(z, FULLV)
  ci <- function(n) quantile(bs[, n], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  one <- function(n) sprintf("%+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]", coef(fit)[[n]], ci(n)[1], ci(n)[2])
  tibble(Threshold = CUTS$label[k], Cells = sum(z$y),
         `Wind residual` = one("WindResid"), `Heat load` = one("HLI"),
         `Shelter` = one("SxMean"))
}) |> bind_rows()

asp_tab |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllll",
                 format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The inherited predictor set had no aspect, so until now the model could not tell a warm slope from a cold one at the same elevation. Adding two aspect-derived terms does three things.

First, it supplies the one piece of thermal information available without a temperature surface. Heat load is positive at every threshold and strengthens steeply with severity (@tbl-aspect). Since heat load is essentially uncorrelated with elevation (@tbl-orthogonality), this is not the elevation gradient under another name: at a given elevation, southwest-facing ground carries heavier mortality than northeast-facing ground. That is the sign cold limitation predicts, and the first evidence here that the thermal axis works independently of elevation.

Second, it leaves the wind coefficient standing. The orthogonalised wind term does not weaken when heat load is controlled for, so whatever it tracks is not the warm-aspect effect in disguise. It is, however, largely the curvature of elevation: this model still enters elevation linearly, and @sec-nonlinear shows the wind term does not survive a flexible basis. Controlling for aspect does not rescue it.

Third, and least comfortably, the two exposure measures disagree. The shelter index is negative, meaning sheltered ground carries *less* attack and exposed ground more, the opposite of what the orthogonalised wind term says and of what @krawchuk2020 predict. The two are only weakly correlated (`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(ZHx$WindResid, ZHx$SxMean))`), so they are not two measurements of one quantity that happen to disagree; they measure different things, and only one is a direct geometric description of exposure. We take this as evidence against treating any single surface as "wind exposure" and reporting its coefficient as though the phrase had one referent. It is also a caution against our own result: the wind residual's negative sign is not corroborated by the one predictor here that describes exposure geometrically rather than by downscaling.

The severe threshold is absent from @tbl-aspect because ten terms and `r sum(ZHx$Severity >= 4)` events drive the fit into quasi-separation, with `r format(sep[["severe+"]], big.mark = ",")` cells at numerically zero fitted probability. The eight-term model of @tbl-ordinal is free of this, which is why it retains its severe row and this one does not.

## Winter temperature thresholds {#sec-cold}

Table S2 summarises the record and Figure S2 maps the network. No station lies inside the analysis grid, and the stations reaching the coldest minima are not the highest ones, which is the point the next paragraph develops.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

st <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/climate/station-winter-minima.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

## The censoring rule is applied here rather than taken on trust from the
## retrieval script. Many older British Columbia Wildfire Service sensors floor
## at exactly -20.0 C. A station-winter is unusable when its minimum sits
## exactly on that floor, because the true minimum is then unknown. A minimum
## colder than the floor shows the sensor did read past it, so readings at
## -20.0 in those winters are real measurements and the winter is kept. The
## floor is a sensor artefact of that network, so the rule does not touch the
## Environment and Climate Change Canada records.
FLOOR <- -20
st$censored <- st$network == "BCWS" &
               abs(st$min_temp_c - FLOOR) < 1e-6 &
               st$n_at_minus20 > 0
stopifnot(identical(st$censored, as.logical(st$censored_flag)))

## Isolated single-observation spikes are rejected at the observation level by
## the retrieval script, which is the only stage holding the sub-daily series a
## per-winter summary cannot carry; `min_temp_c_usable` is that de-spiked
## minimum. Everything else about the screen is visible above.
use <- st[!st$censored & !is.na(st$min_temp_c_usable), ]

## Warm sensor failure. The retrieval screen inspects only the minimum, so a
## sensor that fails warm passes through it invisibly and contributes a
## spuriously mild minimum. NORNS, the highest station in the network at 2,423 m,
## did this through 2015: a February mean daily minimum of +30.0 C and a winter
## "minimum" of +4.6 C. The bias runs towards the conclusion that the landscape
## never gets cold enough, so it is screened here and its effect is reported.
## `build-monthly-climatology.R` derives the monthly means from the same cached
## extracts and carries the flag; the cut is read off that distribution.
clim <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/climate/station-monthly-climatology.csv"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bad_sw <- unique(clim[clim$warm_fail == "TRUE" | clim$warm_fail == TRUE,
                      c("station_name", "winter_year")])
WARM_DROPPED <- nrow(merge(use, bad_sw, by = c("station_name", "winter_year")))
MEAN_HI_RAW  <- mean(use$min_temp_c_usable[use$elevation_m >= 1500])
use <- use[!(paste(use$station_name, use$winter_year) %in%
             paste(bad_sw$station_name, bad_sw$winter_year)), ]
## No physically impossible winter minimum may survive the screen.
stopifnot(max(use$min_temp_c_usable) < 0)

use$band <- cut(use$elevation_m, c(0, 800, 1500, 2500),
                labels = c("below 800 m", "800 to 1,500 m", "above 1,500 m"))
## Held for the supplementary section rather than printed here, so the main
## text keeps to the ten floats the guidelines allow.
SUPP_COLD <- use |> group_by(band) |>
  summarise(Stations = n_distinct(station_name), `Station-winters` = n(),
            `Coldest (°C)` = min(min_temp_c_usable),
            `Mean minimum (°C)` = round(mean(min_temp_c_usable), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllll")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 5.1

stn <- aggregate(cbind(latitude, longitude, elevation_m) ~ station_name,
                 data = st, FUN = function(x) x[1])
coldest_by <- aggregate(min_temp_c_usable ~ station_name, data = use, FUN = min)
stn <- merge(stn, coldest_by, by = "station_name", all.x = TRUE)
stn_sf <- st_transform(st_as_sf(stn, coords = c("longitude","latitude"), crs = 4326), 3005)
xy <- st_coordinates(stn_sf); stn_sf$X <- xy[, 1]; stn_sf$Y <- xy[, 2]
site_bc <- st_transform(st_as_sf(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G))), 3005)
prov_bc <- st_transform(ne_states(country = c("Canada","United States of America"),
                                  returnclass = "sf"), 3005)
bbs <- st_bbox(st_buffer(st_union(c(st_geometry(stn_sf), st_geometry(site_bc))), 25000))
sw  <- unname(bbs["xmax"] - bbs["xmin"])
key <- stn_sf[order(stn_sf$min_temp_c_usable)[1:2], ]

fig_station <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = prov_bc, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = .25) +
  geom_sf(data = site_bc, fill = NA, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = .6) +
```
