```{r}
          colour = "grey20", stroke = .25) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Station\nelevation (m)") +
  geom_label_repel(data = as.data.frame(key), aes(X, Y, label = tolower(station_name)),
                   size = 2, colour = "grey10", fill = "white", alpha = .9,
                   label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(.7, "mm"), box.padding = .5,
                   min.segment.length = 0, segment.colour = "grey30",
                   segment.size = .3, seed = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = bbs["xmin"] + .02*sw,
           y = bbs["ymin"] + .04*(bbs["ymax"] - bbs["ymin"]),
           label = "red outline:\nanalysis grid", size = 1.9, hjust = 0, vjust = 0,
           colour = "#C0392B", fill = "white", alpha = .85,
           label.padding = unit(.7, "mm")) +
  coord_sf(crs = 3005, xlim = bbs[c("xmin","xmax")], ylim = bbs[c("ymin","ymax")],
           datum = st_crs(3005), expand = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(3), labels = km_lab) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(3), labels = km_lab) +
  north + map_theme +
  labs(title = "Weather stations screened for winter minima",
       subtitle = sub_alb)
fig_station
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-station-maps.png", fig_station,
       width = 150, height = 130, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

The cold explanation for the high-elevation suppression assumes it gets cold enough up there to kill beetles. Testing that assumption needs the right threshold, and the threshold is not a single number.

Lethal temperature for this insect depends on the stage overwintering and on when the cold arrives. Cold tolerance is acquired by accumulating glycerol through the autumn and is lost again as the beetle metabolises it in late winter. Larvae are the most tolerant stage, then adults, then pupae, then eggs. Within the larval stages tolerance rises with instar. @safranyik2006chap1 give lethal ranges of -23 to -29 °C for first instars, -23 to -34 °C for second instars, and -29 to -40 °C for third and fourth instars, after Logan and colleagues. The commonly quoted -40 °C is the cold end of the range for the late instars that normally overwinter, not a threshold for the population. The same source is explicit that timing governs the rest: a -30 °C event in midwinter would be expected to kill few beetles, while the same temperature before hardening is complete would kill many.

Assessed against these stage-specific ranges rather than against a single benchmark, the record supports a narrower conclusion.

```{r}
#| label: cold-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false

coldest <- use[which.min(use$min_temp_c_usable), ]
hi      <- use[use$elevation_m >= 1500, ]
lowcold <- use[use$elevation_m < 800, ]
lowcold <- lowcold[which.min(lowcold$min_temp_c_usable), ]

## Date of each winter minimum. Lethal temperature is conditional on the state of
## cold-hardening, so a minimum without a date cannot be compared with a lethal
## range. The per-station-winter summary the fetch writes does not carry the
## timestamp; `add-minimum-dates.R` recovers it from the same cached hourly
## extracts and is documented alongside the fetch.
dates <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/climate/station-winter-minimum-dates.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
useD <- merge(use, dates[, c("station_id","winter_year","min_month","min_date")],
              by = c("station_id","winter_year"))
## The merge must not silently drop or duplicate station-winters.
stopifnot(nrow(useD) == sum(use$network == "BCWS"))
DEC <- 100 * mean(useD$min_month == 12)
```

@fig-climate shows the record three ways: the shape of the winter by elevation band, the year-to-year sequence of minima against the lethal ranges for each overwintering stage, and the ordering of minima by station elevation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-climate
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 8.4
#| fig-cap: "The observational climate record behind the cold check. (a) Winter climograph by elevation band: mean daily maximum, monthly mean and mean daily minimum air temperature, with monthly precipitation as bars rising from the floor of the temperature axis and read against the right-hand scale. Only December, January and February were retrieved, so the shoulder months in which a given temperature is most lethal are absent. The apparent decline of winter precipitation with elevation is a gauge artefact: the high-elevation stations are tipping-bucket instruments, which under-catch snowfall severely, and the bars are shown for the seasonal shape within a band rather than for comparison between bands. (b) Winter minima by year, one point per station-winter, against the lethal ranges reported by @safranyik2006chap1 for first-instar larvae and for the third and fourth instars that normally overwinter. No station-winter enters the late-instar range. (c) The same minima against station elevation, showing that elevation orders them only weakly because cold air pools in the valleys."

MONTH_ORDER <- c(12, 1, 2)
band_of <- function(e) cut(e, c(0, 800, 1500, 2500),
                           labels = c("below 800 m", "800 to 1,500 m", "above 1,500 m"))

cl <- clim[!(clim$warm_fail %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")) & clim$n_days >= 20, ]
cl$band  <- band_of(cl$elevation_m)
cl$month <- factor(cl$month, levels = MONTH_ORDER,
                   labels = c("Dec", "Jan", "Feb"))

## Precipitation is plotted on a secondary axis, so it is rescaled onto the
## temperature axis once here rather than inside the geom.
PR_MAX <- max(tapply(cl$total_precip_mm, list(cl$band, cl$month), mean, na.rm = TRUE),
              na.rm = TRUE)
T_LO   <- -20
PR_SCALE <- abs(T_LO) / PR_MAX

clm <- cl |>
  group_by(band, month) |>
  summarise(tmax = mean(mean_daily_max_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            tavg = mean(mean_temp_c,      na.rm = TRUE),
            tmin = mean(mean_daily_min_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            prcp = mean(total_precip_mm,  na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

## Bars are drawn from the floor of the temperature axis upward. A geom_col here
## would draw from zero downward, so a dry month would render as the tallest bar.
clm$xi <- as.integer(clm$month)

p_clim <- ggplot(clm, aes(month, group = band)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xi - .3, xmax = xi + .3,
                ymin = T_LO, ymax = prcp * PR_SCALE + T_LO),
            fill = "grey82", colour = NA) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = tmin, ymax = tmax), fill = "#2C7FB8", alpha = .18) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmax), colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmin), colour = "#2C7FB8", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tavg), colour = "grey20", linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(aes(y = tavg), colour = "grey20", size = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~band, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Air temperature (°C)", limits = c(T_LO, NA),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ (. - T_LO) / PR_SCALE, name = "Precipitation (mm)")) +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "(a) Winter climograph by elevation band",
       subtitle = "Red: mean daily maximum. Black: monthly mean. Blue: mean daily minimum. Bars: precipitation") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"))

## Lethal ranges are stage-specific and are quoted from the same source the text
## uses, so the figure and the prose cannot drift apart.
leth <- data.frame(
  stage = factor(c("first instar", "third and fourth instars"),
                 levels = c("first instar", "third and fourth instars")),
  lo = c(-29, -40), hi = c(-23, -29))

useP <- use
useP$band <- band_of(useP$elevation_m)

p_series <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = leth, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi,
                             fill = stage), alpha = .18) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("first instar" = "#F39C12",
                               "third and fourth instars" = "#2C7FB8"),
                    name = "Lethal range") +
  geom_point(data = useP, aes(winter_year, min_temp_c_usable, colour = elevation_m),
             size = 1.5, alpha = .9) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Station\nelevation (m)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2015, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Winter (year of January)", y = "Winter minimum (°C)",
       title = "(b) Observed winter minima against stage-specific lethal ranges") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_elev <- ggplot(useP, aes(elevation_m, min_temp_c_usable)) +
  geom_rect(data = leth, inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = stage),
            alpha = .18, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("first instar" = "#F39C12",
                               "third and fourth instars" = "#2C7FB8")) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = winter_year), size = 1.5, alpha = .9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              colour = "grey20", linewidth = .5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Winter") +
  labs(x = "Station elevation (m)", y = "Winter minimum (°C)",
       title = "(c) Winter minimum against station elevation") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

fig_climate <- p_clim / p_series / p_elev + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1, 1))
fig_climate
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-climate.png", fig_climate,
       width = 183, height = 213, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

```{r}
#| label: climate-lapse
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## The lapse rate the record supports, quoted in the text. Reported because the
## alternative to a station record is an assumed lapse rate, and a referee is
## entitled to see what this landscape's own stations give.
lap <- lm(min_temp_c_usable ~ elevation_m, data = use)
LAPSE   <- unname(coef(lap)[2]) * 1000
LAPSE_R2 <- summary(lap)$r.squared
```

Across the screened record the winter minimum falls by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(LAPSE))` °C per 1,000 m of station elevation, and elevation explains `r sprintf("%.2f", LAPSE_R2)` of the variance in it. A predictor that weak cannot carry a thermal explanation on its own, which is the quantitative form of the cold-air pooling the next paragraphs describe.

Across `r nrow(use)` station-winters from `r n_distinct(use$station_name)` stations spanning `r min(use$elevation_m)` to `r max(use$elevation_m)` m, the coldest defensible winter minimum anywhere in the region is `r sprintf("%.1f", coldest$min_temp_c_usable)` °C, at `r tolower(coldest$station_name)` at `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m in winter `r coldest$winter_year`. Above 1,500 m the mean winter minimum is `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(hi$min_temp_c_usable))` °C. No station-winter reaches -35 °C.

That coldest value sits inside the lethal range for first and second instars and at the warm edge of the range for third and fourth. It is not far short of any lethal range. It lies above the range for the stage that normally overwinters and within the range for stages that do not. Whether it killed anything depends on which stages were present, which is a function of the same heat accumulation @sec-aspect is about.

The timing of the minima qualifies this further. Of the Wildfire Service station-winters, `r sprintf("%.0f", DEC)` per cent reach their minimum in December. So do `r sum(useD$min_month[order(useD$min_temp_c_usable)][1:10] == 12)` of the ten coldest, the hardest of them `r sprintf("%.1f", min(useD$min_temp_c_usable[useD$min_month == 12]))` °C on `r format(as.Date(useD$min_date[which.min(ifelse(useD$min_month == 12, useD$min_temp_c_usable, Inf))]), "%e %B %Y")`. December is the front of the hardening window, where a given temperature does more damage than it would in January.

Two further features of the record matter. Elevation orders these minima only weakly: `r tolower(lowcold$station_name)`, at `r format(round(lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m, reaches `r sprintf("%.1f", lowcold$min_temp_c_usable)` °C, within `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(lowcold$min_temp_c_usable - coldest$min_temp_c_usable))` °C of the alpine station `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m - lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m higher. This is consistent with cold-air pooling, and it is the reason temperature cannot be treated as a linear function of elevation on this landscape. And two separate sensor faults were screened out. `r sum(st$censored)` station-winters were set aside because the sensors floor at exactly -20.0 °C, an artefact concentrated before 2008; a naive minimum over those would have manufactured a threshold that is not in the data. A further `r WARM_DROPPED` were set aside for the opposite fault. The retrieval screen inspects only the minimum, so a sensor that fails warm is invisible to it, and the highest station in the network returned a February mean daily minimum of +30.0 °C and a winter "minimum" above freezing at 2,423 m through 2015. Retaining it would have raised the mean minimum above 1,500 m from `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(hi$min_temp_c_usable))` °C to `r sprintf("%.1f", MEAN_HI_RAW)` °C. That bias runs towards the conclusion this section reaches, which is why the screen is applied in the document rather than in the retrieval.

The limits of this check are more extensive than the check itself and are set out in full. The retrieval window runs from 1 December to the end of February, since the script was built to find deep-winter minima. October, November, March and April are absent from the record altogether, and those are precisely the months in which a given temperature is most lethal, before hardening completes or after it reverses. No station inside the study area reported during the outbreak window, and the stations that did report are spread across roughly 100 km of separate massifs. The quantity that actually governs survival is temperature under the bark, not air temperature, and it is observed at landscape scale nowhere.

The defensible conclusion is correspondingly narrow. Deep-winter air temperature in this region does not approach the lethal range for late-instar larvae. That does not establish that freeze mortality is absent, because the record cannot see the shoulder months, cannot see inside the study area, and cannot see under the bark. Cold remains a live mechanism here, alongside the heat-accumulation constraint of @sec-aspect, and this study separates neither from wind.

## Sensitivity to extent {#sec-extent}

The three sections that follow answer objective 4 and test review finding R4, refitting one model across extent, grain and response coding on one dataset.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-extent
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The same model fitted at three extents. As the analysis area shrinks, the share of wind variance explained by elevation rises and the orthogonalised wind coefficient reverses sign. The 2 by 4 km clip is the extent at which the companion study was run."

extent_row <- function(z, lab) {
  r2  <- summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))$r.squared
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y)
  bs  <- block_boot(z)
  q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  ## The block count is reported because it, not the cell count, is the
  ## resampling unit. The clip holds few enough blocks that its interval is
  ## far weaker than its cell count suggests, and the reader must see that.
  tibble(Extent = lab, Cells = nrow(z), Blocks = length(unique(z$block)),
         `R² wind on elevation` = round(r2, 3),
         ## This is the variance inflation the *raw* wind term would carry
         ## against elevation. It is not the VIF of the fitted model, in which
         ## the residualised term is orthogonal to elevation by construction and
         ## its VIF is 1. It is reported to show the collinearity that
         ## orthogonalisation reparameterises away rather than removes.
         `VIF of raw wind` = round(1/(1-r2), 1),
         `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]),
         `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2]))
}
bind_rows(
  extent_row(Z,  sprintf("full landscape (%.0f km²)", nrow(S)*prod(res(G))/1e6)),
  extent_row(ZH, "landscape, host present"),
  extent_row(ZC, sprintf("2 by 4 km clip (%.1f km²)",
                         sum(S$InClip == 1) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6))
) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The confound is a function of extent, and so is the answer. Across the landscape, elevation explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = Z))$r.squared)` per cent of the variance in the wind surface; inside the 2 by 4 km clip it explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = ZC))$r.squared)` per cent (@tbl-extent). The orthogonalised wind coefficient is negative at landscape extent and positive inside the clip.

Two claims live in that table and carry very different weight.

The collinearity result is firm. The share of wind variance elevation explains rises from `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = Z))$r.squared)` across the landscape to `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = ZC))$r.squared)` inside the clip, and that quantity is a property of the two surfaces rather than an estimate with sampling error. It is the mechanism this paper is about, and does not depend on resolving the Krawchuk hypothesis.

```{r}
#| label: clip-interval
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## This interval used to be computed inside an inline expression in the sentence
## below. That hid 150 model refits inside a line of prose, where no reader could
## see the cost and no cache could reach it.
CLIP_BLOCKS <- length(unique(ZC$block))
CLIP_CI     <- local({
  q <- quantile(block_boot(ZC)[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2])
})
```

The sign reversal is a comparison of two point estimates and is not, on this evidence, a demonstrated reversal. The clip contains only `r CLIP_BLOCKS` spatial blocks, so its block interval runs `r CLIP_CI`: it spans zero, and it spans both landscape estimates. By the rule this paper set itself the clip coefficient is not distinguishable from zero, from the landscape estimate, or from its own opposite. What the clip demonstrates is that shrinking the extent destroys the ability to estimate the coefficient at all, a weaker claim than reversal and still damaging for the practice we criticise: a study at this extent would report a positive point estimate with an interval too wide to notice it had learned nothing. Establishing reversal proper would need an extent-by-wind interaction fitted on the pooled data and bootstrapped on common blocks. We have not done that and do not claim it.

## Sensitivity to grain {#sec-grain}

```{r}
#| label: grain-fit
#| cache: true
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Not `tbl-grain-fit`: a `tbl-` prefix declares a float reference target, and this
## chunk sets `output: false`, so Quarto warned "FloatRefTarget with no content".
## The prefix is reserved; a chunk that emits nothing must not claim one.
## The four option lines above must stay above these comments: Quarto only reads
## `#|` options from the top of a cell, and until 2026-08-19 they sat below and
## were silently ignored, so this chunk was neither labelled, cached nor silenced.

CONT <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind","PinePct","Basal")
base_stack <- c(terr[[c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind")]],
                host[[c("PinePct","Basal")]], severity, in_clip)
names(base_stack) <- c(CONT, "Severity", "InClip")

## fact is the aggregation factor from the native 25 m grid.
build_grain <- function(fact) {
  b <- if (fact == 1L) base_stack else
       c(aggregate(base_stack[[CONT]], fact, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE),
         aggregate(base_stack[[c("Severity","InClip")]], fact, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE))
  Gi <- b[["Elevation"]]; rs <- res(Gi)[1]
  w  <- max(3L, as.integer(2 * floor(625 / rs / 2) + 1))   # odd window nearest 625 m
  b$TPI600 <- tpi(Gi, w)
  d <- as.data.frame(b, na.rm = FALSE)
  d$Attacked <- d$Severity > 0
  d$HasHost  <- !is.na(d$PinePct) & d$PinePct > 0
  blk <- max(1L, as.integer(round(BLOCK / fact)))          # blocks stay near 1 km
  rc  <- rowColFromCell(Gi, seq_len(ncell(Gi)))
  d$block <- paste(rc[,1] %/% blk, rc[,2] %/% blk, sep = "_")
  d <- d[complete.cases(d[, MVARS]), ]
  structure(d, res = rs, win = w * rs)
}

grain_row <- function(fact) {
  d  <- build_grain(fact); h <- d[d$HasHost, ]
  z  <- standardise(h)
  r2 <- summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))$r.squared
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y); bs <- block_boot(z)
  q  <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Grain = sprintf("%.0f m", attr(d, "res")),
         `TPI window` = sprintf("%.0f m", attr(d, "win")),
         `Host cells` = nrow(h), Blocks = length(unique(z$block)),
         `R² wind on elevation` = round(r2, 3),
         `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]),
         `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2]),
         `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f",
           mean(sign(bs[, "WindResid"]) == sign(coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]), na.rm = TRUE)))
}

## The 25 m row must reproduce the analysis frame built in `assemble`; if this
## assertion ever fails the two code paths have drifted apart.
stopifnot(nrow(build_grain(1L)) == nrow(S))

SUPP_GRAIN <- bind_rows(lapply(c(1L, 2L, 4L), grain_row)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllllll", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

@work2011, working on carabid beetles, found the apparent importance of terrain derivatives changed with the resolution at which they were computed, because elevation error propagates into derived curvature differently at every grain. The concern transfers directly and is worth separating from extent, which is routinely confused with it.

Here they behave quite differently (Table S3). Aggregating from 25 m to 100 m, a sixteen-fold reduction in cells, leaves the confound essentially untouched: elevation explains close to the same share of wind variance at every grain, and the orthogonalised wind coefficient neither reverses nor decays. The suppression at the top of the gradient is a landscape-scale feature and survives a coarser lens.

The contrast with @sec-extent is the point, and one we should not overstate. Enlarging the cell fourfold changes almost nothing; shrinking the study area destroys the estimate. Grain governs how finely a pattern is resolved, extent governs which part of the joint distribution of elevation and wind the model ever sees, and here only the second mattered.

That is a result about this landscape and this pair of surfaces, not a general ordering of the two axes. @wiens1989 set out the distinction and warned that correlations evident within one domain may disappear or change sign when the extent is enlarged past it, and @dungan2002 recommended that studies report unit size, shape, spacing and extent together for the same reason. The literature since has not settled which axis matters more, and where it has looked it has often found the opposite of what we find: @mcgarigal2016, reviewing several hundred multi-scale habitat studies, concluded that the emphasis on extent may have left grain under-examined. Nor is reporting the weak point we assumed: @estes2018 found resolution and extent reported at closely comparable rates, near three fifths in both cases.

What our result adds is narrower and more useful. @sandel2015 shows that for a genuinely linear relationship the coefficient is extent-independent and only the coefficient of determination moves with extent. A coefficient that changes sign under truncation is therefore a diagnostic for an unmodelled nonlinearity rather than an instance of a general law. That is very likely what is happening here: @fig-gradient shows attack unimodal in elevation while wind rises monotonically, so no monotone wind term can hold across the whole gradient, and the clip lands on one limb of the hump. Read that way the finding is not "extent reverses inferences" but the sharper "truncating a gradient onto one limb of a unimodal response will reverse the apparent sign of anything monotonically correlated with the gradient." Testing it properly means fitting the nonlinearity rather than assuming it away, which is the first thing we would do next.

# Discussion

Read against the review, the result is a negative answer to a question the literature had been answering in the affirmative without measurement. R1 recorded that the wind-disruption mechanism has been invoked as an explanation for years while entering no model; fitted here, on a landscape chosen for its relief, it does not survive a specification that allows the response its observed curvature. R4 recorded that scale is acknowledged but conclusions are not tested against it; tested here, two of three analytical axes change the answer.

Three of the results above are built and then withdrawn, which is deliberate and can be hard to follow on a first reading. We therefore state at the outset what survives.

Four findings stand. Attack is unimodal in elevation. Below 1,900 m the pattern is the distribution of lodgepole pine. Attack rises monotonically with stem diameter and steps at the published source-sink threshold, so host must be coded as size and not only as cover. And above 1,900 m, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*hi_full/hi_alone)` per cent of the suppression remains after every host term we have.

Three do not. The orthogonalised wind coefficient does not survive fitting elevation flexibly. The conclusion that freeze mortality can be excluded does not survive the stage-specific and seasonal structure of lethal temperature. And no estimate at all survives truncating the landscape to a 2 by 4 km clip.

One thing was never established. Nothing here identifies the mechanism behind the high-elevation refugia, and three candidates remain live.

The high-elevation suppression is real, and it is only partly host limitation. Among cells carrying lodgepole pine, attack above `r format(ALPINE, big.mark=",")` m runs at `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(H$Attacked[H$Elevation>=ALPINE]))` per cent against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(H$Attacked[H$Elevation<ALPINE]))` per cent below. Cover barely moves across that step. Stem size does, and @sec-size shows that the share of stands above the source-sink crossover falls roughly four-fold. Conditioning on diameter and the rest of the host set removes `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1 - hi_full/hi_alone))` per cent of the effect on the log-odds scale and leaves the rest standing. Under the @krawchuk2020 definition what remains are refugia: disturbed less severely than the surrounding landscape, with host present, and predictably located by an enduring topographic feature. That matches @cartwright2018 in associating refugia with thinner stands, and it now says something more specific, because thinner here means smaller-stemmed as well as sparser.

We record that the first version of this result rested on cover alone and overstated the case. Reporting cover without diameter concealed a real host effect, and the general lesson is the one this paper keeps arriving at: a host layer is not a single thing, and which attribute of it you use decides the answer.

What we cannot do is attribute the remainder to wind. The ordinal result in @sec-ordinal changes one half of that difficulty and leaves the other where it was.

The statistical half looked, at first, much improved. Once severity is modelled as the ordinal variable it is, the orthogonalised wind term clears the interval test at every threshold above trace and strengthens monotonically with severity. @sec-nonlinear withdraws that reading. Entering elevation flexibly, and residualising wind against the same basis rather than against a straight line, removes between three fifths and seven tenths of the coefficient and leaves no threshold clearing the test. The ordinal coding does recover structure the binary discards, and @krawchuk2020's warning against binary refugia coding stands. But that structure is not attributable to wind: it is very largely the curvature of the elevation response, which the linear specification pushed into the wind term. We therefore do not report a wind effect, in either coding.

The identification half is untouched, and the life history says the competing explanation is more specific than we first allowed.

The upper gradient is where it is coldest, and cold acts on this insect through two separate mechanisms rather than one. The first is overwinter mortality, graded by instar and by the state of cold-hardening [@safranyik2006chap1; @cooke2009mortality]. The second is heat accumulation. A generation must finish in one year, and where summer warmth is insufficient the population becomes semivoltine: it overwinters twice, often in the cold-susceptible early instars, sits longer under natural enemies, and loses the emergence synchrony on which mass attack depends [@safranyik2006chap1; @powell2014].

That second mechanism deserves the emphasis, because it predicts our result without any appeal to wind. Amman's relationship between life-cycle duration, elevation and latitude, reproduced by @safranyik2006chap1, places the ceiling of univoltine development progressively lower as latitude rises, and at the latitude of the Selkirks it falls within the elevation range this study spans. We cannot locate it on this gradient, for reasons the next paragraph gives. But a transition from univoltine to semivoltine ground produces exactly what we observe: a step down in attack, with host present, at an elevation fixed by terrain, and graded in severity because the mechanism acts on how many beetles emerge together.

Cold in either form predicts a dose-response in severity just as wind disruption does. Fewer beetles surviving or emerging in step means both fewer stands attacked and lighter attack in those that are. The monotone strengthening across thresholds is therefore fully consistent with thermal limitation and does nothing to separate it from wind. Orthogonalising against elevation does not orthogonalise against temperature, which is not a linear function of elevation where cold air pools.

We looked for a way out and do not think one exists at this extent. Separating exposure from cold needs a temperature surface whose fine-scale structure is not itself a function of the elevation model, and any surface of the form intercept plus lapse rate times elevation is an affine rescaling of the elevation layer, whatever the lapse rate's source. It is collinear by construction, and only a residual departure from that form would identify anything, which would itself require terrain as the interpolator. The gridded products with genuine sub-kilometre temperature structure all obtain it by regression onto a digital elevation model, so they reproduce the problem rather than solve it.

One result narrows the field, and it narrows it less than we first claimed. @sec-cold shows that deep-winter air temperature in this region does not approach the lethal range for the late-instar larvae that normally overwinter. We had read that as ruling out freeze mortality and leaving heat accumulation as the survivor. It does not go that far. Lethal temperature is stage-specific, and our coldest defensible minimum of `r sprintf("%.1f", coldest$min_temp_c_usable)` °C lies inside the published range for first and second instars. It is also conditional on timing, and `r sprintf("%.0f", DEC)` per cent of our station-winters bottom out in December, at the front of the hardening window. Most decisive, the retrieved record runs only from December to February, so the shoulder months in which a given temperature is most lethal were never observed. Both thermal mechanisms remain live, and we no longer claim to have eliminated either.

Aspect gives partial purchase on one of them. Because heat load is a trigonometric function of the elevation model rather than a field draped over it, it carries thermal information independent of elevation, and @sec-aspect finds it predicts attack severity in the direction warmth-limited development implies. The constraint for which we have an elevation-independent proxy is the heat-accumulation one, and that proxy behaves as the constraint predicts. It says nothing about the overwinter minimum.

The gain is bounded in four ways. The station record is a regional plausibility check, not a temperature surface, since no station inside the study area reported during the outbreak window. Its window excludes the shoulder months. Heat load is a modelled radiation load, not a measured temperature. And none of it touches the possibility that cold-air pooling produces local freeze events the network never sampled, which is precisely the structure @sec-cold shows when a valley station at `r format(round(lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m matches an alpine station `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m - lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m above it.

The deeper obstacle is that the quantity governing overwinter survival is not air temperature but temperature under the bark, which is not observed at landscape scale anywhere. @goodsman2024, validating the standard Canadian Forest Service winter mortality model against observed mortality in Banff National Park, found its spatial predictions poor and attributed the failure to precisely this. The confound we report unresolved is unresolved in this terrain generally, and is not an artefact of our data being thin.

What would resolve it is a degree-day surface for this landscape, and we did not build one. The station archive was retrieved for winter months only, because the question it was assembled to answer was about winter minima. Growing-season accumulation would need the same archive re-streamed across the summer months of eighteen years, and the thresholds to apply are established: emergence scales with degree-days above 14.4 °C, and about 118 degree-days above 4.4 °C carry half a clutch of eggs to hatch in southern British Columbia [@safranyik2006chap1]. That is the first thing we would do next, and it is a data-collection task rather than a design problem.

There is also a class of mechanism that would produce our result without pheromone plumes at all, and the life history makes it more concrete than we first stated. Wind acts on the beetle before it acts on the plume. Bark beetles do not fly in winds exceeding their own flight speed, and *D. ponderosae* flies for shorter periods at 2 m s⁻¹ than at lower speeds in a wind tunnel [@carroll2004bionomics; @jones2019]. Dispersal within a stand is itself wind-structured: beetles drift downwind below the crowns until they meet an attractive plume, then turn and fly upwind to its source [@carroll2004bionomics]. If exposed ground receives fewer arriving beetles, rather than the same number arriving to a disrupted signal, the observable consequence in a static model is identical, and the Allee effect in colonisation means a modest reduction in arrivals can produce a large reduction in successful attack [@powell2014]. We cannot compare our wind values against the flight threshold, because the atlas reports an annual mean at 10 m over open ground and the threshold is an instantaneous below-canopy speed. That mismatch is itself the point: the study's predictor and the insect's constraint are not the same quantity.

The obvious precedent does not settle the direction. @smithmckenna2013, working on white pine blister rust in whitebark pine treeline communities, established that topographic position governs delivery of a wind-borne propagule, but the direction they report is the opposite of the one this alternative needs, with exposed positions favouring *interception* rather than escape. Their agent is a fungus dispersed passively, so neither direction transfers cleanly to a flying insect that selects where it lands. What their result does establish is that the dispersal pathway is a live confound in terrain of this kind. Nothing in our design distinguishes it from pheromone disruption. Doing so would need the dispersal process observed rather than inferred, through attack years, distance from the previous year's attack, or trapping.

One further boundary belongs here, and it is about the insect rather than the terrain. The 1999 to 2015 window is a single epidemic passage. Mountain pine beetle populations move through endemic, incipient-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic phases, and host selection and the spatial configuration of attack are themselves density-dependent [@safranyik2006chap1; @howe2022]. Endemic populations occupy weakened, small-diameter stems, which are distributed quite differently from the large-stemmed stands an epidemic takes. Everything estimated here is therefore beetle behaviour at epidemic density. @krawchuk2020 distinguish refugia by severity from refugia by frequency, and a single outbreak window can speak only to the first.

The honest summary is that we have located candidate refugia, confirmed the host half of the hypothesis in a stronger form than cover alone supports, and cannot support the wind half once elevation is fitted flexibly. The mechanism remains confounded with overwinter mortality, with heat-accumulation limits on voltinism, and with dispersal interception, on the same gradient.

## Host-absence confounding {#sec-lowtrap}

The result that should travel furthest is at the bottom of the gradient. Attack there is near zero, and any refugia mapping exercise lacking a host layer would have identified the valley as a large, spatially coherent, topographically predictable refugium. It is not a refugium. It is a place with almost no pine. Conditioning on host raises attack in the lowest band from `r sprintf("%.1f", grad$"Attacked, all cells (%)"[1])` per cent to `r sprintf("%.1f", grad$"Attacked, host present (%)"[1])` per cent, which is within the range observed at mid elevations.

@krawchuk2020 anticipate this in framing, asking of any candidate refugium both what it is a refugium from and what it is a refugium for, but the framework does not force the check and the data required to perform it are not always at hand. On this landscape the difference between performing it and not is the difference between reporting a roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", sum(S$Elevation < 900) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6)` km2 valley refugium, the modelled ground below 900 m that @tbl-gradient shows carries almost no pine, and reporting none. We would put the requirement more strongly than the framework currently does: a refugium claim without an independent host or habitat layer is not interpretable.

## Terrain limitations

The collinearity result in @sec-extent generalises beyond wind. A fine-resolution climate surface is produced by imposing terrain on a coarse field, so wherever the coarse field is nearly constant the product approaches a function of the terrain. That covers most gridded climate products used in landscape ecology. Three properties govern the severity, and all are checkable before any model is fitted: the ratio of analysis extent to the correlation length of the driving field, the relief of the study area, and which terrain variable does the work in the downscaling, which for wind is elevation and roughness but for radiation would be slope and aspect.

The consequence for synthesis is uncomfortable. If a confound scales with study extent, effect sizes for derived climate predictors are not comparable across studies of different extents, and small studies will systematically report the strongest apparent effects, a pattern easily mistaken for publication bias.

We would ask three things of any study entering such a surface into a disturbance model: report its regression on elevation, report the same diagnostic at more than one extent, and interpret only the orthogonalised coefficient. None requires new data, and here each changed the answer.

Three limitations belong to the host layer specifically. Quadratic mean diameter is a stand-level attribute applied uniformly across a polygon, so it cannot express the within-stand size distribution that decides which individual stems are sources. It is recorded for stems 12.5 cm and over, which is the right domain for this question but means the smallest stands are described by a truncated distribution. And it carries the same 2014 vintage as the species composition, so it too is a post-hoc description of stands the beetle had already reached. The 25 cm crossover we test against is itself an average across studies rather than a constant of this landscape [@carroll2004bionomics], and we use it as a reference point rather than as a fitted threshold.

A fourth limitation is about the insect and not the data. Everything estimated here describes an epidemic population. Endemic populations occupy weakened, small-diameter stems and select hosts differently [@safranyik2006chap1; @howe2022], so the diameter relationship in @sec-size should not be read as a constant of the species.

The plot record calibrates severity but not location, because coordinates for the 28 ground plots were not recoverable. The survey response is observer sketch-mapping with known positional and severity error, and rasterising polygons imposes a grain coarser than the 25 m cell; severity classes are assigned by eye from an aircraft, so the ordinal gradient in @sec-ordinal rests on judgement of proportion killed rather than measurement. The inventory is a modelled operational product whose species percentages are polygon-level attributes applied uniformly. The grain test in @sec-grain spans 25 m to 100 m, which brackets the resolutions in common use and the 900 m2 Landsat grain at which @krawchuk2020 note refugia have typically been described. Finally the analysis is correlational and the outbreak is one epidemic passage; frequency refugia in the sense of @krawchuk2020 cannot be addressed with a single window, and the static design cannot separate a wind effect on pheromone communication from one on dispersal.

The identification gained in @sec-aspect is partial. Heat load bears on the degree-day half of cold limitation, the half governing whether a generation completes in one year. It says almost nothing about the overwinter minimum half, the lethal events that kill larvae outright, which are driven by synoptic air mass intrusions and cold-air pooling rather than by radiation on a slope. Separating warm aspects from cool ones at the same elevation therefore addresses one thermal mechanism and leaves the other untouched, and rests on an assumed functional form, the @mccune2002 equation, rather than an independent measurement.

The shelter index is also imperfect as a test of the mechanism. It is omnidirectional because the Global Wind Atlas supplies no direction, and an omnidirectional index cannot represent a process that depends on where the wind comes from. A directional index on a known prevailing bearing would be sharper, and its disagreement with the wind residual might resolve either way under one.

# Conclusions

Each conclusion below is tied to the review finding it answers. R1 asked whether a mechanism carried in the literature survives being fitted, R3 whether host coded as stem size changes the terrain result, R4 whether the answer is stable across the analyst's free choices, and R5 whether the available wind product measures the quantity the hypothesis concerns.

Beetle-caused mortality at Darkwoods is unimodal across the `r format(round(diff(range(S$Elevation))), big.mark = ",")` m of relief the modelled area spans. Below 1,900 m that pattern is the distribution of lodgepole pine, and conditioning on host removes almost all of it. Above 1,900 m it is not, but the margin is narrower than cover alone implies.

Stem size is the host attribute that matters, and it had not been used. Attack rises monotonically with stand quadratic mean diameter, from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$QMD <= 15]))` per cent in the smallest stands to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*mean(HQ$Attacked[HQ$QMD > 35]))` per cent in the largest, with the steepest step at the 25 cm crossover between beetle sink and beetle source that the species' bionomics predicts [@carroll2004bionomics]. Across the 1,900 m threshold cover is flat while the share of stands above 25 cm falls roughly four-fold. Conditioning on diameter and the remaining host terms removes about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1 - hi_full/hi_alone))` per cent of the high-elevation suppression. The rest stands, and that is where the Krawchuk hypothesis predicts refugia should be.

We do not find a wind effect. The component of the Global Wind Atlas surface orthogonal to a linear elevation term is the strongest negative predictor of attack in host-bearing stands, and modelled as the ordinal severity class it clears the interval test at every threshold above trace. But the response is unimodal, and orthogonalising against a straight line leaves the curvature of elevation inside the wind term. Entering elevation as a quadratic or a spline, and residualising wind against that same basis, collapses the coefficient at every threshold. The apparent wind signal is a specification artefact.

Even had it survived, it would not have been a measurement of the mechanism. Wind arrests bark beetle flight near 2 m s⁻¹, an instantaneous below-canopy speed during a July and August flight window [@carroll2004bionomics; @jones2019]. The atlas supplies an annual mean at 10 m above open ground. Studies that enter such a surface into an insect disturbance model should say which quantity they mean, and we could not.

The thermal alternatives are not eliminated, and we withdraw a stronger claim made earlier. Deep-winter air temperature at every station within 100 km stays clear of the lethal range for the late instars that normally overwinter. It does not stay clear of the range for first and second instars, `r sprintf("%.0f", DEC)` per cent of station-winter minima arrive in December before cold-hardening completes, and the retrieved record excludes October, November and March altogether. Separately, loss of univoltine development at elevation predicts a step down in attack, with host present, at a terrain-fixed elevation, and graded in severity, which is what we observe [@safranyik2006chap1]. A heat load index, being trigonometric in the elevation model and therefore nearly unrelated to elevation, predicts attack at the moderate severity threshold in the direction that constraint implies. But a geometric shelter index computed from the same model carries the opposite sign to the wind residual while being nearly uncorrelated with it, a warning that "wind exposure" is not one measurable thing and that our wind result lacks corroboration from the one predictor describing exposure directly.

The methodological findings are firmer, and all three are failures of design rather than data. Fitted inside a 2 by 4 km clip of the same landscape, elevation explains four fifths of the variance in the wind surface rather than two thirds, the wind coefficient's point estimate turns positive, and its interval widens until it excludes nothing; a four-fold change of grain moves none of this. Extent is the axis that governs whether the coefficient can be estimated here. We do not generalise that ordering: following @sandel2015, the likeliest reading is that truncating a gradient onto one limb of a unimodal response reverses the apparent sign of anything monotonically correlated with it, which is a statement about functional form rather than extent as such. Collapsing severity to attacked or not converts the study's strongest apparent relationship into a null. And without a host layer, the pine-poor valley floor would have been mapped as the largest refugium on the mountain.

# Data availability

Every dataset used here is public and none was collected by the author. Beetle-caused mortality is the British Columbia Aerial Overview Survey pest infestation polygon layer, filtered to `IBM` for 1999 to 2015. Host cover and stand basal area are the provincial Vegetation Resources Inventory layer `VEG_COMP_LYR_R1_POLY`, retrieved from the British Columbia Data Catalogue web feature service. Ambient wind is Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m [@globalwindatlas]. Terrain is derived from the Natural Resources Canada High Resolution Digital Elevation Model [@nrcan2017]. Winter minima are British Columbia Wildfire Service hourly and Environment and Climate Change Canada daily records for stations within 100 km, retrieved by the script named in the Materials section, which also writes the cached per-station-winter summary the manuscript reads.

The analysis is the manuscript. Every table, figure and quoted number is produced by a code chunk in the source document, so rendering it re-runs the pipeline and regenerates the results. The source document and the retrieval scripts are available from the author on request.

# Ethics declarations

This study analysed publicly available spatial and meteorological records only. It involved no human participants, no animal subjects and no sampling of protected species, so ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
